13. Stabilization Policy and the AS/AD Framework

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code

Learning goals

Chapters 11 and 12 built the short-run model from three pieces: the IS curve, the MP curve and the Phillips curve. In those chapters the central bank chose the interest rate case by case. This chapter gives it a rule, and the whole short-run model then fits in one familiar diagram. By the end of it you will be able to:

  • derive the aggregate demand (AD) curve by substituting a monetary policy rule into the IS curve, and read the Phillips curve as an aggregate supply (AS) curve;
  • derive the model’s steady state, its solution for one period, and the rule by which the inflation gap shrinks each period; use them to follow an inflation shock, a disinflation and an aggregate demand shock;
  • read the comparative statics: how the policy response, the slope of the AS curve and the shocks change the first-period effects, the speed of recovery and the total output cost; explain why expectations, credibility and inflation targets matter for the cost of fighting inflation;
  • test the model on U.S. data, and on data for dozens of other countries: policy rates against the policy rule, inflation-output loops, and three centuries of inflation;
  • in Python: write one simulate loop and reuse it in many figures, build tables from lists of dictionaries, reshape data with melt, join tables with merge, and compare two vintages of the same data.

13.1 Model overview

Picture Islandia again, the small island country of the earlier chapters. Its central bank, the Bank of Islandia, no longer decides the interest rate meeting by meeting. It has published a rule instead: when inflation runs above its target the real interest rate goes up, and when inflation runs below it the rate goes down. What does such a rule do when the price of fuel for Islandia’s boats jumps, when islanders go on a spending spree, or when the Bank wants lower inflation for good? This section builds the AS/AD model to answer, and we follow Islandia through every step.

NoteThe big idea

The question. When the central bank sets its interest rate by a fixed rule, how do output and inflation react to a shock, and how does the economy find its way back to normal?

The answer in one sentence. The rule turns the IS curve into a downward-sloping aggregate demand (AD) curve, the Phillips curve is an upward-sloping aggregate supply (AS) curve, and because firms expect last period’s inflation, the AS curve keeps moving until the economy is back at its steady state, with output at potential and inflation on target.

What goes in and what comes out. We choose the inflation target, the policy response, the interest sensitivity of spending, the slope of the Phillips curve and the shocks. The model gives back output and inflation in every period: on impact, on the way back, and in the steady state, together with the total output cost of each episode.

Road map.

  1. The policy rule and the AD curve: the IS curve of Chapter 11 plus a rule for the interest rate.
  2. The Phillips curve as the AS curve: the Phillips curve of Chapter 12, written in levels.
  3. The AS/AD model: steady state and dynamics: the steady state, one period, the path over time, the total output cost, and the chapter’s three events (an inflation shock, a disinflation and a demand shock).
  4. The rule for the nominal interest rate, and richer rules: the rate central banks actually set, and a rule that also watches output.
  5. Expectations and credibility: expectations that look ahead, and why being believed saves output.
  6. Model in code: the key results as Python functions, each checked with numbers. Every later section reuses them.

Notation. A bar over a letter marks a parameter: a number we take from outside the model. Letters without a bar are endogenous variables, which the model determines. The subscript \(t\) counts periods (years).

Symbol Meaning Type
\(\tilde{Y}_t\) short-run output: the percentage gap between actual and potential output endogenous
\(\pi_t\) inflation in period \(t\), in percent endogenous
\(R_t\), \(i_t\) the real and the nominal interest rate endogenous
\(\pi^e_t\) the inflation firms expect for period \(t\) endogenous
\(\bar{\pi}\) the inflation target parameter
\(\bar{m}\) the policy response: how hard the rule leans against inflation parameter
\(\bar{r}\) the marginal product of capital, the normal real interest rate parameter
\(\bar{a}\), \(\bar{b}\) the aggregate demand shock, and the interest sensitivity of spending parameters
\(\bar{\nu}\), \(\bar{o}\) the slope of the Phillips curve, and the inflation shock parameters
\(\bar{x}\) the weight on output in the richer rule (fourth block) parameter
\(c\) credibility, a share between 0 and 1 (fifth block, our addition) parameter
\(\lambda\) our shorthand for \(1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\) (third block) notation
\(\tilde{Y}^*, \pi^*\) a star marks the steady state endogenous
\(\Delta\pi_t\) the change in inflation, \(\pi_t - \pi_{t-1}\) notation

Islandia’s baseline. All worked examples, and every diagram of this notebook, use one set of numbers: an inflation target \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent (the target of most large central banks), the policy response \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) that John Taylor proposed (used again in Fig. 16), the interest sensitivity \(\bar{b} = 2\) of Chapter 11’s example, and an illustrative Phillips-curve slope \(\bar{\nu} = 1\). The shocks are an inflation shock \(\bar{o} = 2\) points for one period, a demand shock \(\bar{a} = 2\) points for nine periods, and a cut in the target from 4 to 2 percent (the numbers of textbook Fig. 13.20).

13.1.1 The policy rule and the AD curve

Assumptions

1. The IS curve (Chapter 11). Islandia’s short-run output depends on the real interest rate \(R_t\):

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,(R_t - \bar{r}).\]

When borrowing costs more than the marginal product of capital \(\bar{r}\), Harbor Boatworks puts off new workshops and islanders put off big purchases, so spending falls below normal. The parameter \(\bar{b} > 0\) says how strongly spending reacts. The aggregate demand shock \(\bar{a}\) moves spending at every interest rate.

2. A monetary policy rule. In Chapter 12 the central bank picked \(R_t\) through the MP curve. Now the Bank of Islandia follows a rule, a fixed recipe that maps what it observes into an interest rate:

\[R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}).\]

Here \(\bar{\pi}\) is the inflation target and \(\bar{m} > 0\) is the policy response. The recipe has two steps: measure how far inflation is from the target, then set the real interest rate \(\bar{m}\) times that many points above \(\bar{r}\). With \(\bar{m} = 1/2\), inflation of 3 percent, one point above the target, calls for a real rate half a point above \(\bar{r}\), and inflation of 1 percent calls for a rate half a point below it. The rule looks at inflation only; the fourth block lets it look at output too.

Solving the model

The rule gives exactly the interest-rate gap \(R_t - \bar{r}\) that appears in the IS curve, so we substitute it (Appendix C.9):

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,\underbrace{(R_t - \bar{r})}_{=\ \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})} = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\,\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}).\]

ImportantKey result: the policy rule and the AD curve

\[R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) \tag{1}\]

\[\text{AD:}\quad \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) \tag{2}\]

The interest rate has dropped out: the AD curve links two endogenous variables, output and inflation.

Islandia in numbers. In the baseline \(\bar{b}\bar{m} = 2 \times 0.5 = 1\). With inflation at 3 percent, the rule sets \(R_t - \bar{r} = 0.5 \times (3 - 2) = 0.5\), and the IS curve turns that into \(\tilde{Y}_t = 0 - 2 \times 0.5 = -1\) percent.

In the diagram output goes on the horizontal axis and inflation on the vertical axis, so we also solve (2) for \(\pi_t\). Move the inflation term to the left and \(\tilde{Y}_t\) to the right, then divide by \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\):

\[\bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) = \bar{a} - \tilde{Y}_t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_t = \bar{\pi} + \frac{\bar{a} - \tilde{Y}_t}{\bar{b}\bar{m}}.\]

So the AD curve is a straight line through the point \((\tilde{Y}, \pi) = (\bar{a}, \bar{\pi})\) with slope \(-1/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\). In the baseline each point of inflation above the target costs Islandia one point of output.

TipIn words: why the AD curve slopes down

The slope comes from the Bank of Islandia, not from shoppers who react to prices as on a market demand curve. When the Bank sees inflation above its target, it raises the real interest rate. Harbor Boatworks and the islanders then spend less, and output drops below potential. A weaker economy pulls inflation down later, and that is exactly what the Bank wants.

What the model predicts

The AD curve is a straight line, so each effect below is the same at every point of it (Appendix C.7):

A change in … effect on \(\tilde{Y}_t\) at a given \(\pi_t\) in the AS/AD diagram
inflation \(\pi_t\), up 1 point \(-\bar{b}\bar{m}\) (baseline \(-1\)) a movement along the AD curve (Fig. 2)
demand shock \(\bar{a}\), up 1 point \(+1\) AD shifts right by 1 point, or up by \(1/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\)
target \(\bar{\pi}\), up 1 point \(+\bar{b}\bar{m}\) AD shifts up by 1 point, or right by \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\)
policy response \(\bar{m}\) or sensitivity \(\bar{b}\), up output reacts more to inflation AD turns around \((\bar{a}, \bar{\pi})\) and gets flatter (Fig. 3)

Two facts are worth keeping:

  • \(\bar{b}\) and \(\bar{m}\) enter only through their product \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\). A tougher central bank and a more interest-sensitive economy give the same AD curve.
  • Inflation on target always goes with \(\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a}\). Whatever \(\bar{m}\) is, with no demand shock the Bank wants output at potential when inflation is on target.

The AD curve slopes down because the central bank leans against inflation, not because buyers dislike high prices.

NoteCheck your understanding

1. Inflation in Islandia reaches 3.5 percent, with no demand shock and the baseline rule. What real-rate gap \(R_t - \bar{r}\) does the Bank of Islandia set, and where does output end up?

Answer

Rule (1) gives \(R_t - \bar{r} = 0.5 \times (3.5 - 2) = 0.75\) points. The AD curve (2) then gives \(\tilde{Y}_t = -2 \times 0.75 = -1.5\) percent: output falls one and a half points below potential.

2. Islandia’s spending becomes twice as sensitive to the interest rate (\(\bar{b}\) doubles), while the Bank keeps its rule. Could the Bank get the same AD curve without that change, just by its own choice?

Answer

Yes. Equation (2) depends on \(\bar{b}\) and \(\bar{m}\) only through the product \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\). Doubling \(\bar{m}\) instead of \(\bar{b}\) doubles the same product, so the AD curve turns to exactly the same flatter line.

13.1.2 The Phillips curve as the AS curve

Assumptions

3. The Phillips curve (Chapter 12). The change in inflation rises with short-run output and with inflation shocks \(\bar{o}\), such as a jump in the price of the fuel that Islandia’s boats burn:

\[\Delta\pi_t \equiv \pi_t - \pi_{t-1} = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}, \qquad \bar{\nu} > 0.\]

4. Adaptive expectations. Firms such as Harbor Boatworks expect this period’s inflation to equal last period’s: \(\pi^e_t = \pi_{t-1}\). When period \(t\) begins, \(\pi_{t-1}\) is already known, so it is a given number for the period, not an unknown.

Solving the model

Write out \(\Delta\pi_t\) and add \(\pi_{t-1}\) to both sides:

\[\pi_t - \pi_{t-1} = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}.\]

ImportantKey result: the AS curve

\[\text{AS:}\quad \pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o} \tag{3}\]

Using \(\pi_{t-1} = \pi^e_t\), it reads \(\pi_t = \pi^e_t + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\): inflation is what firms expected, plus a push from a hot economy, plus any shock. In the diagram it is a straight line with slope \(\bar{\nu}\) that crosses \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) at the height \(\pi_{t-1} + \bar{o}\).

Islandia in numbers. Last year’s inflation was 2 percent and there is no shock. If output runs one point above potential, then with \(\bar{\nu} = 1\) this year’s inflation is \(2 + 1 \times 1 = 3\) percent.

TipIn words: how Harbor Boatworks sets its prices

Harbor Boatworks raises its prices in step with the inflation it expects. When orders pile up and output runs above potential, it pays overtime and runs its slipways harder, so it raises prices faster than that to cover the extra cost. In a slump it raises them more slowly. A fuel shock adds to its costs whatever the state of demand.

What the model predicts

A change in … effect on \(\pi_t\) at a given \(\tilde{Y}_t\) in the AS/AD diagram
output \(\tilde{Y}_t\), up 1 point \(+\bar{\nu}\) a movement along the AS curve
last period’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}\), up 1 point \(+1\) AS shifts up by 1 point, next period too
inflation shock \(\bar{o}\) \(+\bar{o}\) while the shock lasts AS shifts up by \(\bar{o}\) (Fig. 6)
slope \(\bar{\nu}\), up prices react more to booms and slumps AS turns around \((0, \pi_{t-1} + \bar{o})\) and gets steeper

The second row is the engine of the whole chapter. Whenever this period’s inflation differs from last period’s, next period’s AS curve sits at a different height. The AS curve keeps moving until inflation stops changing.

This year’s inflation becomes next year’s expected inflation, so the AS curve keeps moving until inflation stops changing.

NoteCheck your understanding

1. Islandia’s inflation was 2 percent last year. This year output is 1.5 points above potential, and a fuel shock \(\bar{o} = 1\) hits. With \(\bar{\nu} = 1\), what is this year’s inflation?

Answer

The AS curve (3) gives \(\pi_t = 2 + 1 \times 1.5 + 1 = 4.5\) percent: 1.5 points from the boom and 1 point from the fuel shock.

2. Inflation came in at 3 percent this year instead of 2. Why does that matter for next year, even if output is back at potential and fuel prices are normal?

Answer

With adaptive expectations, next year’s AS curve starts from \(\pi_{t-1} = 3\), one point higher (the second row of the table). Even at potential output, inflation then stays at 3 percent unless something pushes it down.

13.1.3 The AS/AD model: steady state and dynamics

Assumptions

5. Equilibrium in every period. In each period \(t = 1, 2, 3, \dots\) both the AD curve (2) and the AS curve (3) hold. The two unknowns are \(\tilde{Y}_t\) and \(\pi_t\). Last period’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}\) and this period’s shocks \(\bar{a}\) and \(\bar{o}\) are given.

6. Shocks are temporary. Both shocks are zero in the long run. For \(\bar{a}\) the reason is the resource constraint: at potential output, the shares of consumption, investment, government purchases and net exports add up to one, so Islandia’s demand cannot stay above normal for ever. Period 0 is the steady state the economy starts from.

Solving the model

Step 1: the steady state. In a steady state there are no shocks (\(\bar{a} = \bar{o} = 0\)) and inflation does not change, \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} = \pi^*\). Put this into the AS curve (3): \(\pi^* = \pi^* + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}^*\), so \(\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}^* = 0\), and since \(\bar{\nu} > 0\), \(\tilde{Y}^* = 0\). Put \(\tilde{Y}^* = 0\) and \(\bar{a} = 0\) into the AD curve (2): \(0 = -\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi^* - \bar{\pi})\), and since \(\bar{b}\bar{m} > 0\), \(\pi^* = \bar{\pi}\).

ImportantKey result: the steady state

\[\tilde{Y}^* = 0, \qquad \pi^* = \bar{\pi} \tag{4}\]

In the long run output is at potential and the central bank’s target becomes the economy’s inflation rate, whatever the values of \(\bar{m}\), \(\bar{b}\) and \(\bar{\nu}\). Islandia’s steady state has inflation of 2 percent and no output gap.

Step 2: one period. Take \(\pi_{t-1}\) as given and substitute the AS curve (3) for \(\pi_t\) in the AD curve (2):

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o} - \bar{\pi}).\]

Multiply out the bracket, keeping the \(\tilde{Y}_t\) term apart:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi} + \bar{o}) - \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t.\]

Move the last term to the left, \(\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t = (1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\tilde{Y}_t\), and divide:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi} + \bar{o})}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.\]

For inflation, subtract \(\bar{\pi}\) from both sides of the AS curve, \(\pi_t - \bar{\pi} = (\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi} + \bar{o}) + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t\), and insert the output solution:

\[\pi_t - \bar{\pi} = (\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi} + \bar{o})\left[1 - \frac{\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}\right] + \frac{\bar{\nu}\bar{a}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}.\]

The bracket equals \(\dfrac{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}} = \dfrac{1}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}}\).

ImportantKey result: output and inflation in one period

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi} + \bar{o})}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}} \tag{5}\]

\[\pi_t - \bar{\pi} = \frac{(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}) + \bar{o} + \bar{\nu}\bar{a}}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}} \tag{6}\]

To keep the formulas short we write \(\lambda \equiv 1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\). This shorthand is ours, not the textbook’s. It lies between 0 and 1.

Islandia in numbers. In the baseline \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 2 \times 0.5 \times 1 = 1\), so \(\lambda = 1/2\).

TipIn words: the Bank splits the pressure

Equation (6) adds up the inflation pressure that reaches Islandia in period \(t\): the gap inherited from last period, plus the inflation shock, plus the push from a demand shock. Only the share \(\lambda\) of it shows up as inflation above the target. The Bank’s rule absorbs the rest by holding output below potential, as equation (5) shows. In the baseline Islandia feels half of the pressure as inflation.

Step 3: the path back to the steady state. Once the shocks are over, set \(\bar{a} = \bar{o} = 0\) in equation (6) and in the AD curve (2), and write \(\lambda\) for the fraction:

ImportantKey result: the path back

\[\pi_t - \bar{\pi} = \lambda\,(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}), \qquad \tilde{Y}_t = -\bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) \tag{7}\]

Each period the inflation gap, and with it the recession, shrinks by the same factor \(\lambda\). In Islandia’s baseline, with \(\lambda = 1/2\), both halve every period.

The first part is a difference equation (Appendix C.10). Apply it again and again, starting from some period \(s\):

\[\pi_t - \bar{\pi} = \lambda(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}) = \lambda^2(\pi_{t-2} - \bar{\pi}) = \dots = \lambda^{t-s}(\pi_s - \bar{\pi}).\]

The fall in the gap from one period to the next is \((\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi}) - (\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) = (1 - \lambda)(\pi_{t-1} - \bar{\pi})\), proportional to the gap itself. So the economy moves fastest when it is farthest from the steady state: the principle of transition dynamics of the Solow model (Chapter 5) holds here too. Because \(\lambda < 1\), the gap always dies out, and the economy always returns to the steady state (4).

Step 4: the total output cost of an episode. Add up the AS curve, \(\pi_t - \pi_{t-1} = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}_t\), over the periods \(t = 1, \dots, T\), writing \(\bar{o}_t\) for the shock of period \(t\). On the left, every middle term cancels:

\[(\pi_1 - \pi_0) + (\pi_2 - \pi_1) + \dots + (\pi_T - \pi_{T-1}) = \pi_T - \pi_0.\]

So \(\pi_T - \pi_0 = \bar{\nu}\sum_t \tilde{Y}_t + \sum_t \bar{o}_t\). Solve for the sum of output:

ImportantKey result: the total output cost

\[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{(\pi_T - \pi_0) - \sum_{t=1}^{T}\bar{o}_t}{\bar{\nu}} \tag{8}\]

Take \(T\) large enough for the economy to be back at a steady state. The total output gained or lost then depends only on how far inflation moved in the end, on the inflation shocks, and on the slope \(\bar{\nu}\). Each point by which inflation must come down costs \(1/\bar{\nu}\) points of a year’s output, a number often called the sacrifice ratio.

The policy response \(\bar{m}\) does not appear in (8). An aggressive central bank makes the slump deeper but shorter, not larger in total.

Step 5: the three events. We now apply equations (5) to (8) to the chapter’s three events, with Islandia’s baseline numbers.

Event 1: an inflation shock. Islandia starts at \(\pi_0 = \bar{\pi} = 2\), and in period 1 only the price of boat fuel jumps, \(\bar{o} = 2\). Equation (6) gives \(\pi_1 - \bar{\pi} = \lambda\bar{o} = 1\), so \(\pi_1 = 3\) percent, and equation (5) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -\bar{b}\bar{m}\lambda\bar{o} = -1\) percent. Inflation rises and output falls: stagflation. From period 2 on, equation (7) halves both gaps: inflation is 2.5, 2.25, 2.125, … percent and output −0.5, −0.25, −0.125, … percent. Inflation ends where it started and the shock adds up to 2, so equation (8) gives a total output loss of \(\sum\tilde{Y}_t = -2/\bar{\nu} = -2\) percent of a year’s output.

Event 2: a disinflation. Islandia starts in a steady state with a target of 4 percent, so \(\pi_0 = 4\). From period 1 on the Bank of Islandia aims at \(\bar{\pi}' = 2\). Every formula above holds with \(\bar{\pi}'\) in place of \(\bar{\pi}\). Equation (6): \(\pi_1 - \bar{\pi}' = \lambda(\pi_0 - \bar{\pi}') = 1\), so \(\pi_1 = 3\) percent, halfway between the old and the new target. The AD curve (2) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_1 - \bar{\pi}') = -1\) percent. After that the gap to the new target halves every period, and the new steady state (4) has \(\pi^* = \bar{\pi}' = 2\). Inflation falls by 2 points in total with no inflation shocks, so by equation (8) the disinflation costs \(-2/\bar{\nu} = -2\) percent of a year’s output.

Event 3: a demand shock. A wave of optimism lifts islanders’ spending, \(\bar{a} = 2\), in periods 1 to 9. In period 1, equation (6) gives \(\pi_1 - \bar{\pi} = \lambda\bar{\nu}\bar{a} = 1\), so \(\pi_1 = 3\) percent, and equation (5) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = \lambda\bar{a} = 1\) percent: a boom with rising inflation. While the shock lasts, inflation drifts toward the point \(C\) where output is at potential. There the AS curve gives \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1}\), so inflation is stable, and the shifted AD curve gives \(0 = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi^c - \bar{\pi})\). Solving for \(\pi^c\):

ImportantKey result: inflation at point C

\[\pi^c = \bar{\pi} + \frac{\bar{a}}{\bar{b}\bar{m}} \tag{9}\]

Islandia in numbers. In the baseline \(\pi^c = 2 + 2/1 = 4\) percent: while the boom lasts, the Bank tolerates inflation two points above its target, because at that rate its rule just offsets the extra spending.

Subtracting \(\pi^c\) from both sides of equation (6) shows that, while \(\bar{a}\) stays constant, the gap \(\pi_t - \pi^c\) also shrinks by the factor \(\lambda\) each period. After eight periods it is \((1/2)^7 \times (3 - 4) \approx -0.008\), so \(\pi_8 \approx 3.992\) percent. When the optimism fades after period 9, equation (7) applies again: \(\pi_{10} - \bar{\pi} = \lambda(\pi_9 - \bar{\pi}) \approx 1\), so inflation is about 3 percent and output about −1 percent, a recession (point \(D\)). From there both gaps halve on the way back to the steady state. Inflation starts and ends at 2 percent with no inflation shocks, so equation (8) gives \(\sum\tilde{Y}_t = 0\): the boom and the later recession cancel exactly.

NoteCheck your understanding

1. A larger fuel shock hits Islandia: \(\bar{o} = 4\) in period 1 only, with the baseline numbers. What are inflation and output in period 1, and what is the total output loss of the whole episode?

Answer

With \(\lambda = 1/2\), equation (6) gives \(\pi_1 - 2 = 0.5 \times 4 = 2\), so \(\pi_1 = 4\) percent. Equation (5) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -1 \times 2 = -2\) percent. Inflation ends back at 2 percent, so by equation (8) the total loss is \(-4/1 = -4\) percent of a year’s output, twice that of Event 1.

2. The Bank of Islandia doubles its policy response to \(\bar{m} = 1\) before the baseline fuel shock \(\bar{o} = 2\) hits. Is the recession in period 1 deeper or milder? Does the total output loss change?

Answer

Now \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 2\) and \(\lambda = 1/3\), so equation (5) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -2 \times 1 \times 2/3 \approx -1.33\) percent: a deeper recession. But the gap now shrinks to a third each period, so it ends sooner. The total, by equation (8), is still \(-2\) percent of a year’s output, because \(\bar{m}\) does not appear in it.

What the model predicts

The first period after a shock. Equations (5) and (6), for an economy that starts in its steady state:

Shock output \(\tilde{Y}_1\) inflation in period 1 baseline what comes next
inflation shock \(\bar{o}\) \(-\bar{b}\bar{m}\lambda\,\bar{o}\) \(\pi_1 - \bar{\pi} = \lambda\bar{o}\) \(-1\) and \(+1\) for \(\bar{o} = 2\) back to the steady state along AD (Figs. 6–9)
target cut from \(\bar{\pi}\) to \(\bar{\pi}'\) \(-\bar{b}\bar{m}\lambda\,(\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')\) \(\pi_1 - \bar{\pi}' = \lambda(\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')\) \(-1\), and \(\pi_1 = 3\) down the new AD curve to \(\bar{\pi}'\) (Figs. 10–11)
demand shock \(\bar{a}\) \(+\lambda\bar{a}\) \(\pi_1 - \bar{\pi} = \lambda\bar{\nu}\bar{a}\) \(+1\) and \(+1\) for \(\bar{a} = 2\) up toward \(\pi^c\), then a slump when it ends (Figs. 12–15)

The role of the parameters. Recall \(\lambda = 1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\), which falls when \(\bar{m}\) or \(\bar{\nu}\) rises.

A higher … recession on impact of \(\bar{o}\), \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\lambda\bar{o}\) speed of return (\(1 - \lambda\)) total output cost, equation (8) inflation at \(C\), equation (9)
policy response \(\bar{m}\) deeper faster unchanged closer to the target
AS slope \(\bar{\nu}\) milder faster smaller, \(1/\bar{\nu}\) per point unchanged

Five predictions.

  • Shocks to prices hurt twice. A one-period fuel shock raises inflation at once, and the Bank then needs a recession lasting many periods to bring it back, because the shock has raised expected inflation.
  • Disinflation is costly when expectations are sticky. Lowering the target permanently lowers inflation, but at a total cost of \((\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')/\bar{\nu}\) points of output.
  • Booms are paid for with recessions. A temporary demand boom leaves inflation above the target. Only a later slump brings it down, and over the whole episode output sums to zero. What remains is a long spell of high inflation, a net loss, which is why central banks try to keep output at potential.
  • Counterclockwise loops. Output above potential pushes inflation up, by the AS curve; inflation above the target makes the central bank push output down, by the AD curve. After the demand shock Islandia goes from \(A\) (0, 2) to \(B\) (1, 3), up toward \(C\) (0, 4), down to \(D\) (−1, 3) and back to \(A\): a counterclockwise loop in the diagram, the pattern tested in Fig. 17.
  • The rule reacts only to inflation. A Bank that could see \(\bar{a}\) directly could offset it with the interest rate and avoid the whole cycle. With a rule based on inflation alone, it reacts to a demand shock only once the shock has raised inflation.

Every gap shrinks by the same factor each period, and the total bill for lower inflation depends only on the slope of the AS curve.

NoteCheck your understanding

1. Suppose the Bank of Islandia had a tougher rule, \(\bar{m} = 1\), during the baseline spending boom \(\bar{a} = 2\). At what inflation rate would Islandia settle while the boom lasts?

Answer

Equation (9) gives \(\pi^c = 2 + 2/(2 \times 1) = 3\) percent, instead of 4 percent with \(\bar{m} = 1/2\). A tougher Bank lets inflation drift less far above its target during the boom.

2. Over the whole demand-shock episode, Islandia’s output adds up to zero. Why is the episode still costly?

Answer

Equation (8) says the boom and the later recession cancel in output. But inflation spends many periods above the 2 percent target, near point \(C\) and on the way back from \(D\). That long spell of high inflation is the net loss, so the Bank would rather keep output at potential.

13.1.4 The rule for the nominal interest rate, and richer rules

Assumptions

7. The Fisher equation (Chapter 8). Central banks set a nominal rate, such as the fed funds rate, and the nominal rate is the real rate plus inflation: \(i_t = R_t + \pi_t\).

8. Taylor’s numbers. John Taylor suggested \(\bar{r} = 2\) percent, \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and \(\bar{\pi} = 2\) percent. We give the Bank of Islandia the same numbers.

9. A rule that also reacts to output. The full Taylor rule adds a term for short-run output, with a weight \(\bar{x} \ge 0\): \(R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) + \bar{x}\tilde{Y}_t\).

Solving the model

The nominal rule. Add \(\pi_t\) to both sides of the rule (1). The left side becomes \(R_t + \pi_t = i_t\):

\[i_t = R_t + \pi_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}).\]

ImportantKey result: the rule for the nominal interest rate

\[i_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) \tag{10}\]

Collecting the terms in \(\pi_t\) gives \(i_t = (\bar{r} - \bar{m}\bar{\pi}) + (1 + \bar{m})\,\pi_t\): the nominal rate moves by \(1 + \bar{m}\) points for each point of inflation.

Islandia in numbers. With Taylor’s numbers, \(\bar{r} - \bar{m}\bar{\pi} = 2 - 1 = 1\) and \(1 + \bar{m} = 1.5\), so \(i_t = 1 + 1.5\,\pi_t\). At the 2 percent target this gives \(i = 4\) percent, which is \(\bar{r} + \bar{\pi}\). At 4 percent inflation it gives \(i = 7\) percent.

Why the slope must exceed one. The nominal rate moves by \(1 + \bar{m}\) points for each point of inflation, so the real rate \(R_t = i_t - \pi_t\) moves by \(\bar{m}\) points. Suppose the nominal rate rose by less than one for one, so that \(\bar{m} < 0\). Then higher inflation would lower the real rate, the AD curve would slope up, and \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} < 0\). If \(-1 < \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} < 0\), then \(\lambda = 1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}) > 1\), and equation (7) makes the inflation gap grow every period. For example, \(\bar{m} = -1/4\) in the baseline gives \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = -1/2\) and \(\lambda = 2\): the gap doubles every period, and inflation spirals away from the target. A good rule therefore raises the nominal rate more than one for one with inflation. Equation (10) also shows a limit of the rule: with Taylor’s numbers it asks for a negative nominal rate, which banks can hardly set, as soon as \(1 + 1.5\,\pi_t < 0\), that is, when inflation falls below \(-2/3\) percent. Chapter 14 comes back to this limit.

TipIn words: the real rate must rise

What moves Islandia’s spending is the real rate, the nominal rate minus inflation. If the Bank of Islandia lifted its nominal rate by less than each rise in inflation, borrowing would get cheaper in real terms just when prices speed up. Spending would rise, inflation would climb further, and the gap would feed on itself. Only a nominal rate that outruns inflation pulls the economy back.

The richer rule. Substitute the rule of assumption 9 into the IS curve:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\left[\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) + \bar{x}\tilde{Y}_t\right] = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) - \bar{b}\bar{x}\,\tilde{Y}_t.\]

Collect the \(\tilde{Y}_t\) terms on the left, \((1 + \bar{b}\bar{x})\tilde{Y}_t\), and divide:

\[\tilde{Y}_t = \frac{\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})}{1 + \bar{b}\bar{x}}.\]

What the model predicts

  • The real rate rises with inflation. With \(\bar{m} > 0\) each point of inflation lifts the nominal rate by more than a point, so the real rate goes up as well. With Taylor’s numbers, one more point of inflation raises the nominal rate by 1.5 points. Fig. 16 tests equation (10) on the fed funds rate.
  • The richer rule keeps every lesson. It gives an AD curve of the same shape, a downward-sloping straight line, but steeper: each point of inflation lowers output by \(\bar{b}\bar{m}/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{x})\) instead of \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\). A demand shock now moves output by only \(\bar{a}/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{x})\): with \(\bar{b} = 2\) and \(\bar{x} = 1/2\) the central bank cancels half of it at once.
  • Even the simple rule watches output, indirectly. Booms raise inflation through the AS curve, and the rule answers the inflation, which is one reason why such a simple rule describes actual policy fairly well.

The nominal rate must outrun inflation, so that the real interest rate climbs whenever prices speed up.

NoteCheck your understanding

1. Islandia’s inflation climbs to 6 percent. With Taylor’s numbers, what nominal rate does the Bank of Islandia set, and what real rate does that imply?

Answer

Equation (10) gives \(i = 1 + 1.5 \times 6 = 10\) percent. The real rate is \(10 - 6 = 4\) percent, which matches rule (1): \(\bar{r} + \bar{m}(\pi - \bar{\pi}) = 2 + 0.5 \times 4 = 4\) percent.

2. A new governor proposes to raise the nominal rate by only 0.75 points for each point of inflation. What would happen to an inflation gap of one point in the baseline?

Answer

A slope of \(1 + \bar{m} = 0.75\) means \(\bar{m} = -1/4\), so \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = -1/2\) and \(\lambda = 2\). By equation (7) the gap doubles every period, to 2, 4, 8 points: inflation spirals away from the target instead of returning.

13.1.5 Expectations and credibility

Assumptions

10. Expected inflation in general. Drop adaptive expectations and keep expected inflation \(\pi^e_t\) in the AS curve:

\[\pi_t = \pi^e_t + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}.\]

11. Rational expectations. Firms use all the information they have to forecast inflation, including the target the central bank announces. An announcement that everyone believes moves \(\pi^e_t\) straight to the new target. In Fig. 20 we measure belief with a credibility share \(c\) between 0 and 1 (our addition): after a cut in the target from \(\bar{\pi}\) to \(\bar{\pi}'\), \(\pi^e = c\,\bar{\pi}' + (1 - c)\,\bar{\pi}\). So when the Bank of Islandia announces a lower target, \(c\) is the share of the cut that Harbor Boatworks builds into its prices.

Solving the model

The algebra of step 2 goes through unchanged, with \(\pi^e_t\) in place of \(\pi_{t-1}\). Equation (5) becomes \(\tilde{Y}_t = \left[\bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi^e_t - \bar{\pi} + \bar{o})\right]/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\), and equation (6) changes in the same way. Take the disinflation from 4 to 2 percent with no shocks. The new target enters the AD curve, and expected inflation is above it by \(\pi^e - \bar{\pi}' = (1 - c)(\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')\).

ImportantKey result: the AS curve with expected inflation, and a credible disinflation

\[\pi_t = \pi^e_t + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o} \tag{11}\]

In period 1 of the disinflation,

\[\tilde{Y}_1 = -\bar{b}\bar{m}\lambda\,(1 - c)(\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}'), \qquad \pi_1 - \bar{\pi}' = \lambda\,(1 - c)(\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}').\]

Islandia in numbers. With the baseline numbers, \(c = 0\) gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -1\) and \(\pi_1 = 3\) (the adaptive case of Event 2), \(c = 1/2\) gives \(-0.5\) and \(2.5\), and \(c = 1\) gives \(0\) and \(2\).

TipIn words: a believed announcement moves the AS curve

When Harbor Boatworks believes the Bank’s new target, it slows its price increases at once. The AS curve then moves down together with the AD curve, and the Bank needs no recession to convince anyone. When nobody believes the Bank, prices keep rising at the old pace, and only a slump brings them down. Credibility decides which of the two worlds Islandia lives in.

What the model predicts

  • A fully credible disinflation is free. When firms believe the new target, the AS curve moves down together with the AD curve, and inflation drops to the new target with output at potential.
  • Every bit of credibility saves output. The recession in period 1 shrinks in proportion to \(1 - c\).
  • Commitment is valuable. A central bank that might later be tempted to create a surprise boom cannot be fully believed (the time consistency problem). Rules, a reputation for low inflation, and announced inflation targets raise credibility and lower the cost of keeping inflation low.
  • Models with fixed expectations can mislead. If a change in policy changes how people form expectations, a model that keeps them fixed gives wrong answers about that policy: this is the Lucas critique.

Being believed is worth output: the more firms trust the new target, the smaller the recession a disinflation needs.

NoteCheck your understanding

1. The Bank of Islandia cuts its target from 4 to 2 percent, and firms give the announcement a credibility of \(c = 3/4\). What are output and inflation in period 1, with the baseline numbers?

Answer

Expected inflation sits \((1 - 0.75) \times 2 = 0.5\) points above the new target. With \(\lambda = 1/2\) and \(\bar{b}\bar{m} = 1\), the box above gives \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -1 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 = -0.25\) percent and \(\pi_1 = 2 + 0.5 \times 0.5 = 2.25\) percent. A quarter of the recession of Event 2 remains.

2. Why can the Bank of Islandia not simply announce the new target and expect full credibility?

Answer

Firms know that, once prices are set, the Bank might be tempted to cut rates for a surprise boom: the time consistency problem. They believe the target only as far as the Bank’s rule, reputation or legal mandate ties its hands, so credibility has to be earned before equation (11) gives a costless disinflation.

NoteRecap
  • The AD curve comes from the policy rule: put \(R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\) into the IS curve and output falls as inflation rises (Fig. 1).
  • The AS curve is the Phillips curve in levels, \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\), and it moves whenever inflation changes (Fig. 5).
  • The steady state has output at potential and inflation on target; after a shock every gap shrinks by the factor \(\lambda = 1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})\) each period (Fig. 9).
  • The total output cost of lowering inflation is \(1/\bar{\nu}\) per point, whatever the policy response; a demand boom is paid back by a later slump (Fig. 11, Fig. 15).
  • A good rule raises the nominal rate more than one for one with inflation, \(i_t = 1 + 1.5\,\pi_t\) with Taylor’s numbers (Fig. 16).
  • Credibility makes disinflation cheaper, and free when it is complete (Fig. 20).

The website cannot run Python, so each interactive figure also gets a version with a precomputed slider. The next helper builds those versions. Run it and move on.

# @title Helper for the website versions (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def slider_figure(make_figure, name, values, start, label=None):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one slider (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure, e.g. a function of Fig. 1
        name        : the argument the slider moves, e.g. "m"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
        label       : the slider's label (the argument name if None)
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a slider that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every curve into one figure; only the start value's are visible
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner = []                          # which precomputed figure each trace is from
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            trace.visible = (i == first)
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one slider step per value: its curves, title, labels and shapes
    steps = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes]}
        visible = [o == i for o in owner]
        steps.append(dict(method="update", label=str(values[i]), args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    fig.update_layout(sliders=[dict(active=first, steps=steps, pad=dict(t=60),
                                    currentvalue=dict(prefix=(label or name) + " = "))])
    return fig

13.2.2 The model as functions

Three Key results hold the whole model: the AD curve, equation (2), the AS curve, equations (3) and (11), and the solution for one period, equations (5) and (6). We write each one as a Python function: a named recipe that takes inputs and gives back a result. The cell also stores Islandia’s baseline numbers, which the functions use whenever we do not pass other values.

# Step 1: Islandia's baseline numbers.
# target pi-bar = 2%, policy response m-bar = 1/2, b-bar = 2, Phillips slope nu-bar = 1
PI_BAR, M_BAR, B_BAR, NU_BAR = 2.0, 0.5, 2.0, 1.0
PI_OLD = 4.0            # the inflation target before the disinflation
A_LAST = 9              # the demand shock lasts from period 1 to period 9
T_MAX = 20              # number of periods simulated after each event


# Step 2: the AD curve.
# `def` creates a function. Its inputs are the arguments in parentheses.
# `m=M_BAR` gives m a default value, used whenever we do not pass one.
# The text in triple quotes describes the function.
def ad_output(pi, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, a=0.0, b=B_BAR):
    """Output on the AD curve at a given rate of inflation.

    Equation (2):  Y~ = a - b m (pi - pi_bar), in percent

    Arguments
        pi     : inflation, in percent (one number or a whole array)
        pi_bar : the inflation target, pi-bar
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        a      : the aggregate demand shock, a-bar
        b      : the interest sensitivity of spending, b-bar
    Returns
        short-run output Y~, in percent
    """
    # `return` gives back the result
    return a - b * m * (pi - pi_bar)


# Step 3: the AS curve
def as_inflation(Y, pi_e=PI_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, o=0.0):
    """Inflation on the AS curve at a given level of output.

    Equations (3) and (11):  pi = pi_e + nu Y~ + o, with expected inflation pi_e
    (pi_e = pi_{t-1}, last period's inflation, in equation (3))

    Arguments
        Y    : short-run output Y~, in percent (one number or a whole array)
        pi_e : expected inflation, in percent
        nu   : the slope of the Phillips curve, nu-bar
        o    : the inflation shock, o-bar
    Returns
        inflation pi, in percent
    """
    # the height of the curve at Y~ = 0 is expected inflation plus the shock
    return pi_e + nu * Y + o


# Step 4: the solution for one period, where the two curves cross
def solve_asad(pi_e, a=0.0, o=0.0, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Output and inflation in one period: the point where the AD and AS curves cross.

    Equations (5) and (6), with expected inflation pi_e in place of pi_{t-1}:
    Y~ = (a - b m (pi_e + o - pi_bar)) / (1 + b m nu), and pi from the AS curve

    Arguments
        pi_e   : expected inflation, in percent
        a, o   : the demand shock a-bar and the inflation shock o-bar
        pi_bar : the inflation target, pi-bar
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        nu     : the slope of the Phillips curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        two numbers: output Y~ and inflation pi, in percent
    """
    # equation (5): output where the curves cross (b-bar is always B_BAR here)
    Y = (a - B_BAR * m * (pi_e + o - pi_bar)) / (1 + B_BAR * m * nu)
    # put that output into the AS curve; a comma returns two results at once
    return Y, as_inflation(Y, pi_e, nu, o)

The events of this chapter play out over many periods. Each period, firms expect last period’s inflation, and the economy jumps to the point where that period’s AD and AS curves cross. The simulation below takes one list of demand shocks \(\bar{a}\) and one list of inflation shocks \(\bar{o}\), one value per period. shock_list builds those lists.

def shock_list(size, last):
    """A list of shocks, one per period: `size` in periods 1 to `last`, zero afterwards.

    The shocks of the chapter's events: o-bar for one period from Fig. 6 on,
    a-bar for nine periods from Fig. 12 on.

    Arguments
        size : the size of the shock, in percentage points
        last : the last period with the shock (0: no shock at all)
    Returns
        a list of T_MAX numbers, one for each period 1, 2, ..., T_MAX
    """
    # Step 1: start with an empty list
    values = []
    # Step 2: `range(1, T_MAX + 1)` counts 1, 2, ..., T_MAX, so the `for` loop runs its
    # indented lines once per period t. `if` runs its lines only when its condition
    # is true, and `else` runs the others otherwise.
    for t in range(1, T_MAX + 1):
        if t <= last:
            # `values.append(x)` adds x at the end of the list `values`
            values.append(size)
        else:
            values.append(0.0)
    return values


NO_SHOCK = shock_list(0.0, 0)                   # T_MAX zeros

simulate repeats the solution for one period, period by period, and returns a table with one row per period.

def simulate(a_list, o_list, pi_start=PI_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """Solve the AS/AD model period by period, with adaptive expectations.

    Each period t, firms expect pi_{t-1}; equations (5) and (6) then give Y~ and pi.
    Period 0 is the old steady state, with inflation pi_start.

    Arguments
        a_list   : the demand shock a-bar in periods 1, 2, ... (a list, e.g. from shock_list)
        o_list   : the inflation shock o-bar in the same periods (a list)
        pi_start : inflation in period 0, in percent
        pi_bar   : the inflation target from period 1 on, pi-bar
        m        : the policy response, m-bar
        nu       : the slope of the Phillips curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a table with one row per period and the columns period, a, o, target, pi_e, Y, pi
    """
    # Step 1: period 0. `dict(period=0, Y=0.0, ...)` is a dictionary: a set of named
    # values. `rows` is a list of dictionaries, one per period.
    rows = [dict(period=0, a=0.0, o=0.0, target=pi_start, pi_e=pi_start, Y=0.0, pi=pi_start)]
    # Step 2: one pass of the loop per period
    for t in range(1, len(a_list) + 1):
        # adaptive expectations: `rows[-1]` is the last element of the list, and
        # `rows[-1]["pi"]` its value named "pi", last period's inflation
        pi_e = rows[-1]["pi"]
        # `Y, pi = ...` unpacks the two results into two variables. The shocks of
        # period t sit at position t - 1, because Python counts from 0.
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, a_list[t - 1], o_list[t - 1], pi_bar, m, nu)
        rows.append(dict(period=t, a=a_list[t - 1], o=o_list[t - 1], target=pi_bar, pi_e=pi_e, Y=Y, pi=pi))
    # Step 3: `pd.DataFrame(rows)` turns the list of dictionaries into a table,
    # one row per dictionary
    return pd.DataFrame(rows)

13.2.3 Checking the key results

The formulas came from algebra. Now we check them with numbers, one Key result at a time, using Islandia’s baseline. First we try solve_asad on two cases: the steady state, and the first period of an inflation shock.

# Step 1: the steady state, with expected inflation equal to the 2% target
Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e=2.0)
# An f-string, f"... {value:.2f}", puts a value into the text;
# ":.2f" means "two decimals".
print(f"Steady state (expected inflation = target = 2%):  Y~ = {Y:.2f}%,  pi = {pi:.2f}%")
# Step 2: an inflation shock o = 2 hits that steady state
Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e=2.0, o=2.0)
print(f"Inflation shock o = 2 hits the steady state:      Y~ = {Y:.2f}%,  pi = {pi:.2f}%")
Steady state (expected inflation = target = 2%):  Y~ = 0.00%,  pi = 2.00%
Inflation shock o = 2 hits the steady state:      Y~ = -1.00%,  pi = 3.00%

In the steady state output is at potential and inflation equals the target. The shock raises inflation by only 1 point, not 2, because the central bank answers with a recession of 1 percent: with \(\lambda = 1/2\), half of the shock becomes inflation (equation 6).

Check 1: the steady state does not depend on the parameters. Equation (4) says that when expected inflation equals the target, output is at potential and inflation stays on target, whatever \(\bar{m}\) and \(\bar{\nu}\) are.

# Three pairs (m-bar, nu-bar), each with expected inflation on target.
# `for m, nu in [...]` takes the pairs in parentheses one at a time and
# unpacks each into two variables, as `Y, pi = ...` does.
for m, nu in [(0.25, 0.5), (0.5, 1.0), (2.0, 2.0)]:
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e=PI_BAR, m=m, nu=nu)
    # equation (4) predicts Y~ = 0 and pi = pi-bar for every pair
    print(f"m = {m:.2f}, nu = {nu:.1f}:  Y~ = {Y:.2f}%,  pi = {pi:.2f}%   (equation 4: Y~ = 0, pi = {PI_BAR:.1f}%)")
m = 0.25, nu = 0.5:  Y~ = 0.00%,  pi = 2.00%   (equation 4: Y~ = 0, pi = 2.0%)
m = 0.50, nu = 1.0:  Y~ = 0.00%,  pi = 2.00%   (equation 4: Y~ = 0, pi = 2.0%)
m = 2.00, nu = 2.0:  Y~ = 0.00%,  pi = 2.00%   (equation 4: Y~ = 0, pi = 2.0%)

Check 2: the gap shrinks by the factor \(\lambda\). We solve the inflation shock period by period with solve_asad, carrying each period’s inflation into the next period’s expectations. Equations (6) and (7) predict an inflation gap of \(\lambda\bar{o}\) in period 1 and \(\lambda^t\bar{o}\) in period \(t\), with output \(-\bar{b}\bar{m}\) times the gap.

# Step 1: `lam`, the share of the inflation gap left after each period
lam = 1 / (1 + B_BAR * M_BAR * NU_BAR)
print(f"Share of the gap left each period: 1 / (1 + b m nu) = {lam:.2f}")
# Step 2: period 0 is the steady state
pi_e = PI_BAR
# Step 3: periods 1 to 6, the simulation against the formula
for t in range(1, 7):
    o = 0.0
    if t == 1:
        o = 2.0         # the inflation shock hits in period 1 only
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, o=o)
    # equations (6) and (7): the gap is lam^t o; `**` means "to the power of"
    gap = lam ** t * 2.0
    print(f"Period {t}: pi = {pi:.4f}% (formula {PI_BAR + gap:.4f}%),  "
          f"Y~ = {Y:+.4f}% (formula {-B_BAR * M_BAR * gap:+.4f}%)")
    # adaptive expectations: this period's inflation replaces the old
    # expectation, ready for the next pass through the loop
    pi_e = pi
Share of the gap left each period: 1 / (1 + b m nu) = 0.50
Period 1: pi = 3.0000% (formula 3.0000%),  Y~ = -1.0000% (formula -1.0000%)
Period 2: pi = 2.5000% (formula 2.5000%),  Y~ = -0.5000% (formula -0.5000%)
Period 3: pi = 2.2500% (formula 2.2500%),  Y~ = -0.2500% (formula -0.2500%)
Period 4: pi = 2.1250% (formula 2.1250%),  Y~ = -0.1250% (formula -0.1250%)
Period 5: pi = 2.0625% (formula 2.0625%),  Y~ = -0.0625% (formula -0.0625%)
Period 6: pi = 2.0312% (formula 2.0312%),  Y~ = -0.0312% (formula -0.0312%)

Check 3: the total output cost. Equation (8) says that the sum of output over a whole episode is \(-\bar{o}/\bar{\nu}\) after an inflation shock and \(-(\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')/\bar{\nu}\) after a disinflation, and that \(\bar{m}\) does not matter. The function below adds up output over 200 periods, long enough to be back at the steady state.

def total_output(o_first=0.0, pi_start=PI_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, periods=200):
    """The sum of output Y~ over a whole episode, to check equation (8).

    The episode is an inflation shock o_first in period 1, or a new target pi_bar.

    Arguments
        o_first  : the inflation shock o-bar in period 1
        pi_start : inflation before the episode, in percent
        pi_bar   : the inflation target during the episode, pi-bar
        m        : the policy response, m-bar
        nu       : the slope of the Phillips curve, nu-bar
        periods  : the number of periods added up
    Returns
        the sum of Y~ over the periods, in percent
    """
    # Step 1: start in the old steady state, with nothing added up yet
    pi_e, total = pi_start, 0.0
    # Step 2: solve each period and add its output to the total
    for t in range(1, periods + 1):
        o = 0.0
        if t == 1:
            o = o_first                         # the shock hits in period 1 only
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, o=o, pi_bar=pi_bar, m=m, nu=nu)
        total = total + Y                       # add this period's output
        pi_e = pi                               # adaptive expectations
    return total


# Step 3: the shock for three slopes nu-bar, then the disinflation for three m-bar
for nu in [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]:
    print(f"Inflation shock o = 2, nu = {nu:.1f}: sum of Y~ = {total_output(o_first=2.0, nu=nu):+.4f}"
          f"   equation (8): {-2.0 / nu:+.4f}")
for m in [0.25, 0.5, 2.0]:
    print(f"Target 4% -> 2%, m = {m:.2f}:       sum of Y~ = {total_output(pi_start=4.0, m=m):+.4f}"
          f"   equation (8): {(2.0 - 4.0) / NU_BAR:+.4f}")
Inflation shock o = 2, nu = 0.5: sum of Y~ = -4.0000   equation (8): -4.0000
Inflation shock o = 2, nu = 1.0: sum of Y~ = -2.0000   equation (8): -2.0000
Inflation shock o = 2, nu = 2.0: sum of Y~ = -1.0000   equation (8): -1.0000
Target 4% -> 2%, m = 0.25:       sum of Y~ = -2.0000   equation (8): -2.0000
Target 4% -> 2%, m = 0.50:       sum of Y~ = -2.0000   equation (8): -2.0000
Target 4% -> 2%, m = 2.00:       sum of Y~ = -2.0000   equation (8): -2.0000

Check 4: inflation at point \(C\). Keep the demand shock \(\bar{a} = 2\) in place for 60 periods. Equation (9) predicts that inflation settles at \(\bar{\pi} + \bar{a}/(\bar{b}\bar{m})\) with output back at potential: 4 percent in the baseline and 3 percent with \(\bar{m} = 1\).

# For the baseline m-bar and for m-bar = 1: 60 periods of a demand shock a = 2
for m in [0.5, 1.0]:
    pi_e = PI_BAR
    for t in range(1, 61):                       # a shock a = 2 that does not end
        Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, a=2.0, m=m)
        pi_e = pi
    # the last period against equation (9)
    print(f"m = {m:.1f}: after 60 periods pi = {pi:.4f}%, Y~ = {Y:+.4f}%"
          f"   equation (9): pi_c = {PI_BAR + 2.0 / (B_BAR * m):.4f}%")
m = 0.5: after 60 periods pi = 4.0000%, Y~ = +0.0000%   equation (9): pi_c = 4.0000%
m = 1.0: after 60 periods pi = 3.0000%, Y~ = +0.0000%   equation (9): pi_c = 3.0000%

Check 5: the nominal rule and why its slope must exceed one. With Taylor’s numbers, equation (10) should agree with \(i = 1 + 1.5\,\pi\), and the real rate \(i - \pi\) should rise by \(\bar{m} = 0.5\) for each point of inflation. Then we give the central bank a wrong-signed response, \(\bar{m} = -1/4\), start one point above the target, and watch the gap: with \(\lambda = 2\) it should double every period.

# Step 1: the nominal rate of equation (10) at four inflation rates, with r-bar = 2%
r_bar = 2.0
for pi in [0.5, 2.0, 4.0, 6.0]:
    i = r_bar + pi + M_BAR * (pi - PI_BAR)       # equation (10)
    print(f"pi = {pi:.1f}%:  i = {i:.2f}%  (1 + 1.5 pi = {1 + 1.5 * pi:.2f}%),  real rate i - pi = {i - pi:.2f}%")

# Step 2: a wrong-signed response, starting one point above the target
pi_e = PI_BAR + 1.0
for t in range(1, 5):
    # with m = -0.25 the nominal rate rises by only 0.75 per point of inflation
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, m=-0.25)
    print(f"m = -0.25, period {t}: inflation gap = {pi - PI_BAR:.2f} points")
    pi_e = pi
pi = 0.5%:  i = 1.75%  (1 + 1.5 pi = 1.75%),  real rate i - pi = 1.25%
pi = 2.0%:  i = 4.00%  (1 + 1.5 pi = 4.00%),  real rate i - pi = 2.00%
pi = 4.0%:  i = 7.00%  (1 + 1.5 pi = 7.00%),  real rate i - pi = 3.00%
pi = 6.0%:  i = 10.00%  (1 + 1.5 pi = 10.00%),  real rate i - pi = 4.00%
m = -0.25, period 1: inflation gap = 2.00 points
m = -0.25, period 2: inflation gap = 4.00 points
m = -0.25, period 3: inflation gap = 8.00 points
m = -0.25, period 4: inflation gap = 16.00 points

Check 6: the richer rule. With \(\bar{x} = 1/2\), a demand shock \(\bar{a} = 2\) and inflation on target, the formula above gives \(\tilde{Y} = 2/(1 + 2 \times 0.5) = 1\) percent. We plug that output into the rule and the resulting interest rate into the IS curve: the IS curve must give back the same output.

# Step 1: demand shock, weight on output, inflation on target
a, x, pi = 2.0, 0.5, PI_BAR
# Step 2: output on the richer AD curve
Y = (a - B_BAR * M_BAR * (pi - PI_BAR)) / (1 + B_BAR * x)
# Step 3: the richer rule gives the interest rate gap R - r_bar
rate_gap = M_BAR * (pi - PI_BAR) + x * Y
print(f"Richer AD curve at pi = target: Y~ = {Y:.2f}%   (simple rule: {ad_output(PI_BAR, a=a):.2f}%)")
# Step 4: the IS curve with that interest rate must give back the same output
print(f"IS curve with that interest rate: Y~ = a - b (R - r_bar) = {a - B_BAR * rate_gap:.2f}%")
Richer AD curve at pi = target: Y~ = 1.00%   (simple rule: 2.00%)
IS curve with that interest rate: Y~ = a - b (R - r_bar) = 1.00%

Check 7: credibility. For the cut in the target from 4 to 2 percent, period 1 should give \(\tilde{Y}_1 = -\bar{b}\bar{m}\lambda(1 - c) \times 2\): −1, −0.5 and 0 percent for credibility 0, 1/2 and 1.

# For credibility c = 0, 1/2 and 1: period 1 of the cut in the target to 2%
for c in [0.0, 0.5, 1.0]:
    # expected inflation after the announcement (equation 11)
    pi_e = c * 2.0 + (1 - c) * PI_OLD
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, pi_bar=2.0)
    # the formula for period 1; + 0.0 turns -0.0 into 0.0
    formula = -B_BAR * M_BAR * lam * (1 - c) * (PI_OLD - 2.0) + 0.0
    print(f"credibility {c:.1f}: expected pi = {pi_e:.1f}%  ->  pi = {pi:.2f}%, Y~ = {Y:+.2f}%  (formula {formula:+.2f}%)")
credibility 0.0: expected pi = 4.0%  ->  pi = 3.00%, Y~ = -1.00%  (formula -1.00%)
credibility 0.5: expected pi = 3.0%  ->  pi = 2.50%, Y~ = -0.50%  (formula -0.50%)
credibility 1.0: expected pi = 2.0%  ->  pi = 2.00%, Y~ = +0.00%  (formula +0.00%)

Last, we try simulate on the inflation shock of Figs. 6 to 9 and show its first six periods.

# the inflation shock: o = 2 in period 1 only, no demand shock. `.head(6)` keeps the
# first six rows of the table, and `.round(3)` rounds every number to three decimals.
simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(2.0, 1)).head(6).round(3)
period a o target pi_e Y pi
0 0 0.0 0.0 2.0 2.000 0.000 2.000
1 1 0.0 2.0 2.0 2.000 -1.000 3.000
2 2 0.0 0.0 2.0 3.000 -0.500 2.500
3 3 0.0 0.0 2.0 2.500 -0.250 2.250
4 4 0.0 0.0 2.0 2.250 -0.125 2.125
5 5 0.0 0.0 2.0 2.125 -0.062 2.062

Inflation jumps to 3 percent in period 1, then falls to 2.5, 2.25, 2.125, …; the gap to the 2 percent target halves every period, and so does the recession. The column target is the inflation target behind each period’s AD curve, and pi_e is expected inflation, the height of that period’s AS curve at \(\tilde{Y} = 0\).

13.2.4 Drawing and data tools

The AS/AD diagrams share a few drawing tools, and the data figures at the end of the chapter share tools that give each country a fixed color and build the website’s country menus. Run them and move on, or open the box to see how they work.

NoteShow the drawing and data tools

Every diagram uses the same axes and the same few drawing steps, so we write them once:

  • add_ad and add_as draw one curve and write its name at its right end;
  • add_point marks a point with dashed guides to the axes, and add_arrow draws an arrow;
  • asad_figure starts a figure with one or two panels, and asad_axes fixes the axes and writes the title.

The first cell sets the grids and the fixed axes, and draws a curve with its name at its end.

# @title Drawing tools: grids, fixed axes and a curve with its name
# Step 1: the grids. `np.linspace(-15, 15, 241)` creates 241 evenly spaced numbers
# from -15 to 15, one every 0.125. Our model functions work on a whole array at
# once, so one call gives a whole curve.
Y_GRID = np.linspace(-15, 15, 241)          # output levels for the AS curves
PI_GRID = np.linspace(12, -5, 137)          # inflation, high to low, for the AD curves
# Step 2: fixed axes, so that you can see the curves move
X_RANGE, PI_RANGE = [-4, 4], [-1, 8]
FADED = "rgba(0,128,112,0.35)"              # light teal: AS curves of earlier periods


def axis_names(col):
    """The names Plotly gives the axes of a panel: x and y in panel 1, x2 and y2 in panel 2.

    Arguments
        col : the panel, 1 or 2
    Returns
        the names of its horizontal and vertical axes
    """
    # `if` without `else`: the second `return` runs only for panels after the first
    if col == 1:
        return "x", "y"
    return f"x{col}", f"y{col}"


def add_curve(fig, x, y, label, color, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw one curve in a panel and write its name at its last point inside the axes.

    Arguments
        fig   : the figure to draw on
        x, y  : the points of the curve (arrays)
        label : the curve's name, e.g. "AD" ("" for none); HTML such as "AS<sub>2</sub>" writes AS2
        color : its color, e.g. TEAL
        dash  : "solid" or "dash"
        col   : the panel to draw in, 1 or 2
    """
    # Step 1: draw the curve; `add_trace(..., row=1, col=2)` draws in the second panel
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=x, y=y, mode="lines", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             line=dict(color=color, width=3, dash=dash)), row=1, col=col)
    # Step 2: the points inside the axes; `&` is true where both conditions hold
    inside = (x >= X_RANGE[0]) & (x <= X_RANGE[1]) & (y >= PI_RANGE[0]) & (y <= PI_RANGE[1])
    # Step 3: the name at the last point inside: `x[inside]` keeps the values where
    # `inside` is true, and `[-1]` takes the last of them
    if inside.any() and label != "":
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x[inside][-1], y=y[inside][-1], xref=xref, yref=yref, text=label,
                           showarrow=False, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", font=dict(color=color, size=14))

The next tools draw the two curves of the model, a point with its guides, and an arrow.

# @title Drawing tools: the AD and AS curves, points and arrows
def add_ad(fig, label, color, a=0.0, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, b=B_BAR, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw an AD curve: output on the horizontal axis, inflation on the vertical axis.

    Equation (2), computed by ad_output

    Arguments
        fig, label, color : the figure, the curve's name and its color
        a, pi_bar, m, b   : the demand shock and the parameters of the AD curve
        dash, col         : the line style and the panel
    """
    # the AD curve gives output for each inflation rate of PI_GRID
    add_curve(fig, ad_output(PI_GRID, pi_bar, m, a, b), PI_GRID, label, color, dash, col)


def add_as(fig, label, color, pi_e=PI_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, o=0.0, dash="solid", col=1):
    """Draw an AS curve.

    Equation (3), computed by as_inflation

    Arguments
        fig, label, color : the figure, the curve's name and its color
        pi_e, nu, o       : expected inflation, the slope and the inflation shock
        dash, col         : the line style and the panel
    """
    # the AS curve gives inflation for each output level of Y_GRID
    add_curve(fig, Y_GRID, as_inflation(Y_GRID, pi_e, nu, o), label, color, dash, col)


def add_point(fig, Y, pi, label, col=1, guides=True):
    """Mark the point (Y, pi) with a dot and a label, and dashed lines to both axes.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        Y, pi  : output and inflation at the point
        label  : the point's name, e.g. "A" ("" for none)
        col    : the panel
        guides : True draws the dashed guides to the axes
    """
    # Step 1: the guides start far outside the chart: the axes cut them off at
    # their edges, wherever these are
    if guides:
        fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[-100, Y, Y], y=[pi, pi, -100], mode="lines", showlegend=False,
                                 hoverinfo="skip", line=dict(color="black", width=1, dash="dash")),
                      row=1, col=col)
    # Step 2: the dot
    fig.add_trace(go.Scatter(x=[Y], y=[pi], mode="markers", name=label, showlegend=False,
                             marker=dict(color="black", size=10)), row=1, col=col)
    # Step 3: the label, well above the dot and a little to the right: clear of the
    # curves and the dashed guides through it
    if label != "":
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=Y, y=pi, xref=xref, yref=yref, text=label, showarrow=False, xanchor="left",
                           yanchor="bottom", xshift=4, yshift=8, font=dict(size=16))


def add_arrow(fig, x0, y0, x1, y1, col=1):
    """Draw an arrow from (x0, y0) to (x1, y1) in axis units; none if the two points almost coincide.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure to draw on
        x0, y0 : where the arrow starts
        x1, y1 : where it points
        col    : the panel
    """
    # draw it only if the two points are visibly apart
    if abs(x1 - x0) + abs(y1 - y0) > 0.15:
        xref, yref = axis_names(col)
        fig.add_annotation(x=x1, y=y1, ax=x0, ay=y0, xref=xref, yref=yref, axref=xref, ayref=yref, text="",
                           showarrow=True, arrowhead=3, arrowwidth=2, arrowcolor="black")

The last two drawing tools start a figure and set its axes. The axes stay fixed for every slider setting except a few extreme ones, where asad_axes widens them so that no dot falls off the chart.

# @title Drawing tools: an empty figure and fixed axes that widen only when needed
def asad_figure(cols=1, titles=None):
    """An empty figure with one or more panels side by side.

    Arguments
        cols   : the number of panels
        titles : one short title per panel (None for none)
    Returns
        the empty Plotly figure
    """
    # `make_subplots(rows=1, cols=2)` creates a figure with two panels side by side
    fig = make_subplots(rows=1, cols=cols, subplot_titles=titles, horizontal_spacing=0.1)
    # `update_annotations(yshift=16)` moves every text already in the figure (here only
    # the panel titles) 16 pixels up, clear of curve labels at the top edge
    fig.update_annotations(yshift=16)
    return fig


def asad_axes(fig, title, panels=1):
    """Fixed AS/AD axes in the first panels (no tick in the bottom-left corner) and the title.

    Arguments
        fig    : the figure
        title  : the title, with the readout of the chosen values
        panels : the number of panels that get the AS/AD axes
    """
    # Step 1: widen an axis only if a dot would fall off the chart. `fig.data` is the
    # list of traces already drawn; `min` and `max` give the smaller and the larger
    x_range, pi_range = list(X_RANGE), list(PI_RANGE)
    for trace in fig.data:
        if trace.mode == "markers":
            x_range = [min(x_range[0], trace.x[0] - 0.5), max(x_range[1], trace.x[0] + 0.5)]
            pi_range = [min(pi_range[0], trace.y[0] - 0.4), max(pi_range[1], trace.y[0] + 0.8)]
    # Step 2: round ticks on the usual axes; on wider axes, `tickvals=None` lets
    # Plotly choose the ticks itself
    x_ticks, pi_ticks = list(range(-3, 4)), list(range(0, 8))
    if x_range != X_RANGE or pi_range != PI_RANGE:
        x_ticks, pi_ticks = None, None
    # Step 3: the same axes in every panel, then the title and the legend
    for col in range(1, panels + 1):
        fig.update_xaxes(title_text="Output, Ỹ (percent)", range=x_range, tickvals=x_ticks, zeroline=False,
                         row=1, col=col)
        fig.update_yaxes(title_text="Inflation, π (percent)", range=pi_range, tickvals=pi_ticks,
                         zeroline=False, row=1, col=col)
    fig.update_layout(title=title, legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top",
                                               bgcolor="rgba(255,255,255,0.8)"))

The data figures at the end of this chapter (Figs. 16–21) can go beyond the textbook’s economies: the same series exist for many other countries. The file countries.csv lists every economy in the chapter’s multi-country files, with its region and whether it belongs to the OECD. We give each country a fixed color, so that it keeps its color when you add or remove others, and two countries that are shown together never share a color. The next cell builds the palette.

# @title Data tools: the color palette
# Step 1: 24 dark colors and 20 more, without the ones too pale on a white page
LIGHT = ["#F7E1A0", "#E2E2E2", "#FBE426", "#16FF32", "#1CFFCE", "#2ED9FF"]
PALETTE = list(px.colors.qualitative.Dark24)
for color in px.colors.qualitative.Alphabet:
    if color not in LIGHT:
        PALETTE.append(color)
# Step 2: this blue is close to the U.S. navy: move it to the end.
# `PALETTE.index(c)` finds the position of color c, `.pop(i)` removes the item at
# that position and returns it, and `.append` puts it at the end.
PALETTE.append(PALETTE.pop(PALETTE.index("#2E91E5")))

group_colors walks through the countries one by one and gives each the first color that suits it.

# @title Data tools: a color for each country
def group_colors(names, groups, fixed=None):
    """A color for each country that no other country of its groups uses, as far as the palette allows.

    Arguments
        names  : the countries, in the order they get their colors
        groups : lists of countries shown together (the website menus)
        fixed  : {country: color} for the book's countries (None for none)
    Returns
        a dictionary {country: color}
    """
    colors = dict(fixed or {})
    for name in names:
        # Step 1: a country with a fixed color keeps it; `continue` goes on to the next
        if name in colors:
            continue
        # Step 2: the colors of the countries already shown with this one.
        # `colors.get(other)` is the color of `other`, or None if it has none yet.
        used = []
        for group in groups:
            if name in group:
                for other in group:
                    used.append(colors.get(other))
        # Step 3: free colors are not used in its groups; new colors by no country
        free, new = [], []
        for color in PALETTE:
            if color not in used:
                free.append(color)
                if color not in colors.values():
                    new.append(color)
        # Step 4: `new + free + PALETTE` joins three lists and `[0]` takes the first
        # item: a color no country uses yet if there is one, else one free in its groups
        colors[name] = (new + free + PALETTE)[0]
    return colors

The website shows the OECD members and eight large emerging economies, so those countries get their colors first.

# @title Data tools: the countries and their colors
# Step 1: the list of countries, and the groups the menus show
countries = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "countries.csv")
G7 = ["Canada", "France", "Germany", "Italy", "Japan", "United Kingdom", "United States"]
EMERGING = ["Argentina", "Brazil", "China", "India", "Indonesia", "Russia", "Saudi Arabia", "South Africa"]
BOOK_COLORS = {"United States": BLUE, "United Kingdom": TEAL, "Euro area": GREEN, "Japan": "#5aa0d8"}
OECD_PLUS = list(BOOK_COLORS) + sorted(set(countries.country[countries.oecd]) - set(BOOK_COLORS)) + EMERGING
# Step 2: `countries.groupby("region")` hands over each region's name with its rows,
# so `regions` becomes a list of country lists, one per region
regions = []
for region, rows in countries.groupby("region"):
    regions.append(list(rows.country))
# Step 3: the colors, first for the OECD and emerging economies, then for the rest
rest = sorted(set(countries.country) - set(OECD_PLUS))
INFLATION_COLORS = group_colors(OECD_PLUS + rest, [OECD_PLUS] + regions, BOOK_COLORS)
