missing_or_off writes a short note for a chart title when a chosen country has no data or leaves the chart.

# @title Data tools: a title note for countries without data or off the chart
def missing_or_off(part, column, countries, low, high):
    """Title text naming the chosen countries without data, and those whose values leave the chart.

    Countries with no data in `part`, and countries whose values leave [low, high].

    Arguments
        part      : the data table shown in the chart
        column    : the column on the vertical axis
        countries : the chosen countries
        low, high : the range of the vertical axis
    Returns
        the note, e.g. "; no data: Chile", or "" when every country fits
    """
    # Step 1: sort the countries; `values.empty` is true when a selection has no rows
    missing, off = [], []
    for name in countries:
        values = part[column][part.country == name]
        if values.empty:
            missing.append(name)
        elif values.min() < low or values.max() > high:
            off.append(name)
    # Step 2: the note; `", ".join(names)` glues the names into one text,
    # with a comma between them
    note = ""
    if missing:
        note += "; no data: " + ", ".join(missing)
    if off:
        note += "; off the chart: " + ", ".join(off)
    return note

The website versions of the multi-country figures need two more helpers: a menu that switches between countries, and buttons that list one group of countries in the legend. Run the two cells and move on.

# @title Helpers for the website country menus (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def compact(fig):
    """Shrink a website figure, so that the saved notebook stays small.

    Short dates, 4 significant digits and a short hover text.

    Arguments
        fig : a Plotly figure
    Returns
        the same figure, smaller
    """
    for trace in fig.data:
        # Step 1: dates as short text
        x = pd.Series(trace.x if trace.x is not None else [], dtype=object).infer_objects()
        if pd.api.types.is_datetime64_any_dtype(x):
            trace.x = x.dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist()
        # Step 2: numbers with 4 significant digits
        if trace.y is not None and np.asarray(trace.y).dtype.kind == "f":
            trace.y = [float(f"{v:.4g}") for v in trace.y]
        # Step 3: a short hover text for the lines
        if "lines" in (trace.mode or "") and trace.hovertext is None:
            trace.hovertemplate = "%{fullData.name}<br>%{x}: %{y}<extra></extra>"
    return fig


def menu_figure(make_figure, name, values, start):
    """Join precomputed versions of a figure with one dropdown menu (the website cannot run Python).

    Arguments
        make_figure : the function that draws the figure
        name        : the argument the menu chooses, e.g. "country"
        values      : the values of that argument to precompute
        start       : the value shown first
    Returns
        one Plotly figure with all versions and a menu that shows one at a time
    """
    # Step 1: draw the figure once for every value
    figures = [make_figure(**{name: v}) for v in values]
    first = values.index(start)
    # Step 2: copy every trace into one figure; only the start value's are shown
    fig = go.Figure(layout=figures[first].layout)
    owner, shown = [], []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        for trace in f.data:
            shown.append(True if trace.visible is None else trace.visible)
            trace.visible = shown[-1] if i == first else False
            fig.add_trace(trace)
            owner.append(i)
    # Step 3: one menu entry per value: its traces, title, labels, shapes and axes
    buttons = []
    for i, f in enumerate(figures):
        layout = {"title": f.layout.title.to_plotly_json(),
                  "annotations": [a.to_plotly_json() for a in f.layout.annotations],
                  "shapes": [s.to_plotly_json() for s in f.layout.shapes],
                  "legend.title.text": f.layout.legend.title.text,
                  "xaxis.range": f.layout.xaxis.range, "yaxis.range": f.layout.yaxis.range}
        visible = [shown[j] if o == i else False for j, o in enumerate(owner)]
        buttons.append(dict(label=str(values[i]), method="update", args=[{"visible": visible}, layout]))
    # Step 4: the menu, above the plot
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=110), updatemenus=[dict(type="dropdown", buttons=buttons, active=first,
                                                            x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom")])
    return compact(fig)
# @title Helper for the website group buttons (run this cell; you do not need to read it)
def group_menu(fig, book, small=8):
    """Buttons that list one group of countries in the legend; the countries in `book` are always drawn.

    Arguments
        fig   : a Plotly figure with one trace per country
        book  : the textbook's countries, always drawn
        small : a group with at most this many countries is drawn at once
    Returns
        the same figure, with the buttons
    """
    # Step 1: the countries of each group, with short names for the regions
    names = [t.name for t in fig.data]
    short = {"Europe and Central Asia": "Europe", "Asia and Pacific": "Asia-Pacific",
             "Middle East and Africa": "Africa, Mideast"}
    groups = {"Textbook": list(book), "G7": G7, "Americas": [], "Europe": [], "Asia-Pacific": [],
              "Africa, Mideast": []}
    for c, r in zip(countries.country, countries.region):
        if c in names:
            groups[short.get(r, r)].append(c)
    # a short legend lists every country
    first = ["legendonly" if len(names) <= 40 else False] * len(names)
    # Step 2: one button per group: drawn, in the legend only, or hidden
    buttons = []
    for label, members in groups.items():
        # skip a group with no country in the figure
        if not set(members) & set(names):
            continue
        visible = []
        # the textbook countries are always drawn; the group's are drawn or listed
        for j, n in enumerate(names):
            if n in book:
                visible.append(True)
            elif n in members:
                visible.append(True if len(members) <= small else "legendonly")
            else:
                visible.append(first[j] if label == "Textbook" else False)
        buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="restyle", args=[{"visible": visible}]))
    # Step 3: start with the first button, and add the buttons above the plot
    for trace, v in zip(fig.data, buttons[0]["args"][0]["visible"]):
        trace.visible = v
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(t=120), updatemenus=list(fig.layout.updatemenus) + [dict(
        type="buttons", direction="right", x=0, y=1.02, xanchor="left", yanchor="bottom", buttons=buttons)])
    return compact(fig)

13.3 Monetary policy rules and the AD curve

We combine the IS curve with the central bank’s rule to get the AD curve, then see how the strength of the policy response changes its slope.

Fig. 1: The aggregate demand curve

Goal. Build the AD curve from the IS curve and the policy rule, and see what each parameter does to it.

\[\left.\begin{array}{ll} \text{IS curve:} & \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}(R_t - \bar{r}) \\ \text{Policy rule:} & R_t - \bar{r} = \bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}) \end{array}\right\} \Rightarrow \text{AD curve: } \tilde{Y}_t = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_t - \bar{\pi})\]

The AD curve slopes down, but not for the reason a demand curve for hamburgers does. It describes the central bank: when inflation is above target, the rule raises the real interest rate, investment falls, and output falls below potential. As with the IS curve, output goes on the horizontal axis.

The dot marks the point where inflation equals the target. There the interest-rate term is zero and output is \(\tilde{Y} = \bar{a}\): with no demand shock, potential output. When you change a parameter, the baseline curve stays behind as a dashed gray line.

The function below draws the figure. It needs only ad_output from Model in code, so all of its code is drawing code: open it to see how the curves, the dot and the title are placed.

Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 1, the AD curve
def ad_curve(pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, b=B_BAR, a=0.0):
    """The AD curve, with the point where inflation equals the target.

    Draws Fig. 1 (adapted from Fig. 13.1 in Jones). When a parameter differs from the
    baseline, the baseline AD curve stays behind as a dashed gray line.

    Arguments
        pi_bar : the inflation target, pi-bar
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        b      : the interest sensitivity of spending, b-bar
        a      : the aggregate demand shock, a-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    fig = asad_figure()
    # Step 1: the baseline curve, dashed gray, only when a parameter has changed.
    # `!=` means "is not equal to", and comparing two groups of numbers in
    # parentheses checks them all at once
    if (pi_bar, m, b, a) != (PI_BAR, M_BAR, B_BAR, 0.0):
        label = "AD (baseline)"
        # no baseline label when the new AD, or its own label, would run into it:
        # `x > 2.4 and y < 4.3` is true only when both conditions hold
        if (
            ad_output(-1.0, pi_bar, m, a, b) > 2.4
            and ad_output(-0.3, pi_bar, m, a, b) < 4.3
        ):
            label = ""
        add_ad(fig, label, GRAY, dash="dash")
    # Step 2: the new AD curve, and the dot where inflation equals the target
    add_ad(fig, "AD", BLUE, a, pi_bar, m, b)
    add_point(fig, a, pi_bar, "π = π̄")
    # Step 3: the title reports the AD equation and output at the target
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"AD: Ỹ = {a:.1f} − {b * m:.2f} × (π − {pi_bar:.1f});   "
        f"at π = π̄ = {pi_bar:.1f}%, Ỹ = {a:.1f}%",
    )
    return fig
# Fig. 1 with sliders. `interact` turns each argument of ad_curve into a slider,
# and draws the figure again every time you move one. The `;` at the end only
# hides an extra line of text.
interact(
    ad_curve,
    pi_bar=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=5.0, step=0.5,
                       description="inflation target π̄ (%)", style=WIDE),
    m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25,
                  description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
    b=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.5, max=4.0, step=0.5,
                  description="interest sensitivity b̄", style=WIDE),
    a=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-3.0, max=3.0, step=0.5,
                  description="demand shock ā", style=WIDE),
);
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 1 with a precomputed slider for the demand shock
# one picture of Fig. 1 per value of a-bar; the slider shows one at a time
slider_figure(
    ad_curve,
    "a",
    [-2.0, -1.0, 0.0, 1.0, 2.0],     # the values of a-bar
    start=0.0,
    label="demand shock ā",
)

Source. Adapted from Fig. 13.1 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The slope depends on the product \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\): each point of inflation above target costs \(\bar{b}\bar{m} = 1\) point of output in the baseline. Raise \(\bar{m}\) or \(\bar{b}\) and the curve becomes flatter.
  • A demand shock \(\bar{a}\) and a new target \(\bar{\pi}\) shift the curve: \(\bar{a}\) moves it right or left, \(\bar{\pi}\) up or down. The dot always sits at \((\bar{a}, \bar{\pi})\).
  • A change in inflation itself does not shift the curve; it is a movement along it (Fig. 2).

Your turn. The central bank raises its target from 2 to 3 percent. At an inflation rate of 3 percent, what output does the AD curve now give, compared with the baseline? Check with the sliders and with ad_output.

Hint

Compare ad_output(3.0) with ad_output(3.0, pi_bar=3.0). A higher target means the central bank sees less “excess” inflation at any given rate.

# Your turn: try it here

Fig. 2: The AD curve after an inflation shock

Goal. See why higher inflation moves the economy along the AD curve instead of shifting it.

The economy starts in steady state at point \(A\): inflation at the 2 percent target, output at potential. Now inflation jumps to \(\pi' = 3\) percent. The policy rule raises the real interest rate by \(\bar{m}(\pi' - \bar{\pi}) = 0.5\) points, investment falls, and output falls to point \(B\). The readout in the title follows the chain: inflation, then the interest rate, then output. Figs. 2 and 3 share one function.

First we compute the two numbers of the readout. move_along_ad applies the policy rule, equation (1), and then the AD curve, equation (2): the rise in the real interest rate, and output at \(B\).

def move_along_ad(pi_new, m):
    """The policy response and output when inflation moves from the target to pi_new.

    Equation (1):  R - r-bar = m-bar (pi' - pi-bar); then equation (2), the AD curve,
    gives output at point B

    Arguments
        pi_new : the new inflation rate, pi', in percent
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
    Returns
        rate : the rise in the real interest rate, R - r-bar, in points
        Y_B  : output at point B, Y~, in percent
    """
    # the policy rule: the real interest rate rises by m-bar per point of inflation
    rate = m * (pi_new - PI_BAR)
    # the AD curve: output at the new inflation rate
    Y_B = ad_output(pi_new, m=m)
    return rate, Y_B
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Figs. 2 and 3, a movement along the AD curve
def inflation_rises(pi_new=3.0, m=M_BAR):
    """The AD curve when inflation rises from the target to pi_new: a move from A to B.

    Draws Figs. 2 and 3 (adapted from Figs. 13.2 and 13.3 in Jones). When m is not
    the baseline value, the baseline AD curve stays behind as a dashed gray line.

    Arguments
        pi_new : the new inflation rate, pi', in percent
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (move_along_ad)
    rate, Y_B = move_along_ad(pi_new, m)
    fig = asad_figure()
    # Step 2: the baseline AD curve, dashed gray, only when m-bar has changed
    if m != M_BAR:
        label = "AD (m̄ = 0.5)"
        # no label when the new AD would run into it
        if ad_output(-1.0, m=m) > 2.4 and ad_output(-0.3, m=m) < 4.3:
            label = ""
        add_ad(fig, label, GRAY, dash="dash")
    # Step 3: the AD curve, point A, and point B (no second letter on top of A)
    add_ad(fig, "AD", BLUE, m=m)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, PI_BAR, "A")
    if pi_new != PI_BAR:
        add_point(fig, Y_B, pi_new, "B")
    # Step 4: two arrows: inflation rises (on the left) ...
    add_arrow(fig, -3.7, PI_BAR, -3.7, pi_new)
    # ... so output falls (at the bottom)
    add_arrow(fig, 0.0, -0.6, Y_B, -0.6)
    # Step 5: the title follows the chain: inflation, interest rate, output
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"π: {PI_BAR:.1f} → {pi_new:.1f}%   ⇒   R − r̄ = {rate:.2f}   ⇒   "
        f"Ỹ: 0.00 → {Y_B:.2f}%",
    )
    return fig
# Fig. 2 with sliders for the new inflation rate and the policy response
interact(
    inflation_rises,
    pi_new=FloatSlider(value=3.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5,
                       description="new inflation rate π′ (%)", style=WIDE),
    m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25,
                  description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
);
Show the code of the website version 
# @title Website version: Fig. 2 with a precomputed slider for the new inflation rate
# one picture of Fig. 2 per value of the new inflation rate
slider_figure(
    inflation_rises,
    "pi_new",
    [1.0, 1.5, 2.0, 2.5, 3.0, 3.5, 4.0, 5.0],     # the values of pi'
    start=3.0,
    label="new inflation rate π′ (%)",
)

Source. Adapted from Fig. 13.2 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Only the point moves; the curve stays put. Inflation of 3 percent brings output to 1 percent below potential.
  • Move \(\pi'\) below 2 percent: the central bank cuts the real interest rate and output rises above potential.
  • The rule works through the real interest rate: \(R - \bar{r}\) in the title is the size of the policy response.

Key numbers: the policy rule

The textbook’s example: with \(\bar{m} = 1/2\), inflation 2 points above target raises the real interest rate by 1 point. Through the AD curve, that costs \(\bar{b} \times 1 = 2\) points of output.

13.4 Aggregate supply and the AS/AD diagram

Next comes the AS curve, the Phillips curve in levels. Putting it next to the AD curve gives the diagram that solves the model and shows its steady state.

Fig. 4: The aggregate supply curve

Goal. Read the Phillips curve as an upward-sloping aggregate supply curve.

\[\pi_t = \pi_{t-1} + \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}\]

At the start of period \(t\), last year’s inflation \(\pi_{t-1}\) is already known. So the Phillips curve is a relation between this year’s inflation and output. When output is above potential, firms work overtime to meet demand, and they raise their prices by more than usual to cover the extra costs: inflation rises. The curve crosses \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) at \(\pi_{t-1}\) (plus any inflation shock \(\bar{o}\)), so it shifts whenever inflation changes.

The function below draws the AS curve with add_as. It needs only as_inflation from Model in code, so all of its code is drawing code.

Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 4, the AS curve
def as_curve(pi_prev=PI_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, o=0.0):
    """The AS curve, which crosses Y~ = 0 at last year's inflation plus the shock.

    Draws Fig. 4 (adapted from Fig. 13.4 in Jones). When a parameter differs from the
    baseline, the baseline AS curve stays behind as a dashed gray line.

    Arguments
        pi_prev : last year's inflation, pi_{t-1}, in percent
        nu      : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
        o       : the inflation shock, o-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    fig = asad_figure()
    # Step 1: the baseline curve, dashed gray, only when a parameter has changed
    if (pi_prev, nu, o) != (PI_BAR, NU_BAR, 0.0):
        label = "AS (baseline)"
        # no label when the two labels at the right edge would overlap
        if abs(as_inflation(4.0, pi_prev, nu, o) - 6.0) < 0.6:
            label = ""
        add_as(fig, label, GRAY, dash="dash")
    # Step 2: the new AS curve, and the dot where it crosses Y~ = 0
    add_as(fig, "AS", TEAL, pi_prev, nu, o)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_prev + o, "")
    # Step 3: the title reports the AS equation and inflation at Y~ = 0
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"AS: π = {pi_prev:.1f} + {nu:.2f} × Ỹ + {o:.1f};   "
        f"at Ỹ = 0, π = {pi_prev + o:.1f}%",
    )
    # room for the label "AS (baseline)" at the right edge
    fig.update_layout(margin=dict(r=120))
    return fig
# Fig. 4 with sliders for last year's inflation, the slope and the shock
interact(
    as_curve,
    pi_prev=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=0.0, max=6.0, step=0.5,
                        description="last year's inflation π_{t−1} (%)", style=WIDE),
    nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25,
                   description="slope ν̄", style=WIDE),
    o=FloatSlider(value=0.0, min=-2.0, max=3.0, step=0.5,
                  description="inflation shock ō", style=WIDE),

What to notice.

  • Last year’s inflation and the shock \(\bar{o}\) move the curve up and down, one for one.
  • \(\bar{\nu}\) turns the curve around the dot: a steeper curve means prices react more to a boom or a slump.
  • Because \(\pi_{t-1}\) is expected inflation, the AS curve carries expectations into the diagram. That is the key to every event below.

Fig. 5: The AS/AD framework

Goal. Put the two curves in one diagram and find the short-run equilibrium, and the steady state.

This diagram is the whole short-run model: the inputs are the parameters (\(\bar{\pi}\), \(\bar{m}\), \(\bar{\nu}\)) and expected inflation, the outcomes are this period’s output and inflation. In a steady state inflation does not change, so \(\pi_t = \pi_{t-1}\). The AS curve then requires \(\tilde{Y}^* = 0\), and the AD curve then requires \(\pi^* = \bar{\pi}\): inflation on target and output at potential. The readout tells you whether the crossing point is a steady state.

First the economics. short_run_point solves the model for one period, equations (5) and (6), and checks whether the crossing point is a steady state, equation (4).

def short_run_point(pi_e, pi_bar, m, nu):
    """The short-run equilibrium, and whether it is a steady state (Fig. 5).

    Equations (5) and (6) give the point where AS and AD cross; by equation (4), it
    is the steady state only when expected inflation equals the target

    Arguments
        pi_e   : expected inflation, pi_{t-1}, in percent
        pi_bar : the inflation target, pi-bar
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        nu     : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        Y, pi : output Y~ and inflation pi where the curves cross, in percent
        state : "the steady state" or "not a steady state"
    """
    # where the AS and AD curves cross (solve_asad)
    Y, pi = solve_asad(pi_e, pi_bar=pi_bar, m=m, nu=nu)
    # a steady state needs pi_t = pi_{t-1}, so expected inflation must equal the target
    state = "the steady state"
    if pi_e != pi_bar:
        state = "not a steady state"
    return Y, pi, state
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 5, the AS/AD diagram
def asad_diagram(pi_e=PI_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS and AD curves and the short-run equilibrium where they cross.

    Draws Fig. 5 (adapted from Fig. 13.5 in Jones).

    Arguments
        pi_e   : expected inflation, pi_{t-1}, in percent
        pi_bar : the inflation target, pi-bar
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        nu     : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the numbers of the figure (short_run_point)
    Y, pi, state = short_run_point(pi_e, pi_bar, m, nu)
    # Step 2: the two curves, and the dot where they cross
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_as(fig, "AS", TEAL, pi_e, nu)
    add_ad(fig, "AD", BLUE, pi_bar=pi_bar, m=m)
    add_point(fig, Y, pi, "")
    # Step 3: the title says whether the crossing point is a steady state
    asad_axes(fig, f"AS and AD cross at Ỹ = {Y:.2f}%, π = {pi:.2f}%: {state}")
    return fig
# Fig. 5 with sliders for expected inflation and the three parameters
interact(

                     description="expected inflation π_{t−1} (%)", style=WIDE),

                       description="inflation target π̄ (%)", style=WIDE),
    m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25,
                  description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),

What to notice.

  • When expected inflation equals the target, the curves cross at \((0, \bar{\pi})\) whatever \(\bar{m}\) and \(\bar{\nu}\) are.
  • Raise expected inflation to 4 percent: the AS curve shifts up, inflation rises and output falls. The crossing is not a steady state, because inflation will differ from what firms expected, and the AS curve will move again next period. The next figures follow that movement.
  • AD slopes down because of the central bank; AS slopes up because of firms’ pricing. Neither is a market demand or supply curve.

13.5 Event 1: an inflation shock

A one-time jump in inflation, such as an oil price spike, hits an economy in its steady state. We follow the AS/AD diagram period by period as the economy finds its way back.

Fig. 6: The initial response to an inflation shock

Goal. See the first period of Event #1: an inflation shock, such as a lasting rise in the price of oil.

The shock \(\bar{o} = 2\) hits for one period only. It shifts the AS curve up by 2 points, from AS to AS₁. If output stayed at potential, inflation would rise one for one, to 4 percent. But the policy rule fights the higher inflation with a higher interest rate, so the economy slides down the AD curve, from \(A\) to \(B\): inflation rises and output falls at the same time. This is stagflation, the U.S. experience after the oil shocks of the 1970s.

Figs. 6 to 9 show the same event at different periods, so we write one function. It simulates the event with simulate and draws period t: the AS curves of the earlier periods in light teal, the current one in full color, and the path so far, with the textbook’s letters (\(B\), \(C\), \(D\) for periods 1, 2, 3).

The three cells below hold that function and its two helpers, add_event_curves and add_event_path, which the later events reuse. They only call simulate and the drawing tools, so all of their code is drawing code.

Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Figs. 6 to 15, the AS and AD curves of an event
def add_event_curves(fig, path, t, as_periods, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR, col=1):
    """The curves of a simulated event at period t.

    The original AS curve, the AS curves of as_periods (the last one solid, the
    earlier ones light teal), and every AD curve up to period t (today's in blue,
    the older ones dashed gray). Used by Figs. 6 to 15.

    Arguments
        fig        : the figure to draw on
        path       : the simulated event, a table from simulate
        t          : the period shown
        as_periods : the periods whose AS curves are drawn
        m          : the policy response, m-bar
        nu         : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
        col        : the panel, 1 or 2
    """
    # Step 1: the original AS and today's. `path.pi_e[s]` is the value of the column
    # pi_e in the row of period s; today's AS crosses Y~ = 0 at pi_e + o
    first, last = path.pi_e[0], as_periods[-1]
    today = path.pi_e[last] + path.o[last]
    # two AS labels closer than this would overlap (a steep AS exits at the top)
    near = 0.6 * max(1, nu)
    same = today == first
    # Step 2: the original AS: solid teal if it is today's, dashed gray otherwise,
    # with no label on top of today's label. `"AS" if c else ""` picks the first
    # value when the condition c holds, the second otherwise
    old_label = "AS" if same or abs(today - first) > near else ""
    color, dash = (TEAL, "solid") if same else (GRAY, "dash")
    add_as(fig, old_label, color, first, nu, dash=dash, col=col)
    # Step 3: the AS curves of as_periods, except those equal to the original AS
    for s in as_periods:
        start = path.pi_e[s] + path.o[s]
        if start != first:
            # a label on the last one, and on the first one if it is far enough away
            named = s == last or (s == as_periods[0] and abs(start - today) > near)
            label = f"AS<sub>{s}</sub>" if named else ""
            color = TEAL if s == last else FADED     # the earlier ones light teal
            add_as(fig, label, color, path.pi_e[s], nu, path.o[s], col=col)
    # Step 4: every AD curve up to period t, each one once. `drawn` lists the pairs
    # (a, target) already drawn; `x in some_list` is true when x is one of them
    drawn = []
    for s in range(t + 1):
        pair = (path.a[s], path.target[s])
        if pair not in drawn:
            drawn.append(pair)
            name = "AD" if s == 0 else f"AD<sub>{s}</sub>"
            # how far this AD lies from today's: 0 for today's AD
            shift = abs(pair[0] - path.a[t] + B_BAR * m * (pair[1] - path.target[t]))
            # no label when an old label would sit on today's label
            if 0 < shift * min(1, 1 / (B_BAR * m)) < 0.6:
                name = ""
            # today's AD in blue, the older ones dashed gray
            color, dash = (BLUE, "solid") if shift == 0 else (GRAY, "dash")
            add_ad(fig, name, color, pair[0], pair[1], m, dash=dash, col=col)
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Figs. 6 to 15, the path of an event
def add_event_path(fig, path, t, letters, col=1):
    """The economy's path from A (period 0) to period t.

    Dots, an arrow from each period to the next, and the textbook's letters.
    Used by Figs. 6 to 15.

    Arguments
        fig     : the figure to draw on
        path    : the simulated event, a table from simulate
        t       : the last period drawn
        letters : {period: letter}, the textbook's letters, e.g. {1: "B"}
        col     : the panel, 1 or 2
    """
    # Step 1: point A, the old steady state of period 0
    add_point(fig, path.Y[0], path.pi[0], "A", col)
    # Step 2: one arrow and one dot per period
    for s in range(1, t + 1):
        add_arrow(fig, path.Y[s - 1], path.pi[s - 1], path.Y[s], path.pi[s], col)
        # with no shock, no letter on top of A
        moved = (path.Y[s], path.pi[s]) != (path.Y[0], path.pi[0])
        if s in letters and moved:
            add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], letters[s], col)
        else:
            add_point(fig, path.Y[s], path.pi[s], "", col, guides=False)
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Figs. 6 and 8, the economy t periods after an inflation shock
# the textbook's letters for periods 1-3
SHOCK_LETTERS = {1: "B", 2: "C", 3: "D"}


def inflation_shock(o=2.0, t=1, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS/AD diagram t periods after a one-period inflation shock o.

    Draws Figs. 6 and 8 (adapted from Figs. 13.6 and 13.8 in Jones).

    Arguments
        o  : the inflation shock in period 1, o-bar
        t  : the period shown
        m  : the policy response, m-bar
        nu : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: simulate the event: the shock o hits in period 1 only
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(o, 1), m=m, nu=nu)
    # Step 2: the curves of periods 1 to t, and the path so far
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_event_curves(fig, path, t, list(range(1, t + 1)), m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, t, SHOCK_LETTERS)
    # Step 3: the title reports period t. `path.loc[t]` is the row of period t, and
    # `now.pi` its value in the column pi. `round(x, 2) + 0.0` rounds to two
    # decimals; adding 0.0 turns a rounded -0.0 into 0.0, so no title shows "-0.00"
    now = path.loc[t]
    Y_now = round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {Y_now:.2f}%   "
        f"(shock ō = {o:.1f} in period 1 only)",
    )
    return fig

    nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25,

);

Source. Adapted from Fig. 13.6 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The shock of 2 points raises inflation by only 1 point, to 3 percent, because output falls by 1 percent. Half of the shock shows up as inflation, half as recession, since \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\).
  • Raise \(\bar{m}\): the central bank fights harder, so inflation rises less and the recession is deeper.
  • A negative \(\bar{o}\) (say, a fall in oil prices) gives the mirror image: lower inflation and a boom.

Fig. 7: Two periods after an inflation shock

Goal. See why the AS curve does not jump back after the shock ends.

In period 2 the shock is over, \(\bar{o} = 0\). But firms now expect last period’s inflation, \(\pi_1 = 3\) percent. So the new curve AS₂ crosses \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) at \(\pi_1\), above the original AS (panel a). High inflation raised expected inflation, and expectations adjust only slowly: inflation is sticky. In panel (b) the economy moves from \(B\) to \(C\): inflation falls a little, and the central bank lets output recover a little, though it stays below potential.

The function below draws the two panels. It simulates the event with simulate, as in Fig. 6, so all of its code is drawing code.

Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 7, two periods after an inflation shock
def two_periods(o=2.0, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS curve of period 2 (a) and the move from B to C (b).

    Draws Fig. 7 (adapted from Fig. 13.7 in Jones).

    Arguments
        o  : the inflation shock in period 1, o-bar
        m  : the policy response, m-bar
        nu : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: simulate the event: the shock o hits in period 1 only
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(o, 1), m=m, nu=nu)
    # Step 2: two panels; `for col in [1, 2]:` draws the same curves in both
    fig = asad_figure(
        2,
        (
            "(a) Period 2: the AS curve moves to AS<sub>2</sub>",
            "(b) Period 2: the Fed steers the economy to C",
        ),
    )
    for col in [1, 2]:
        add_event_curves(fig, path, 2, [1, 2], m, nu, col)
    # Step 3: panel (a): the path to B, and a dot where AS2 crosses Y~ = 0, at pi_1
    add_event_path(fig, path, 1, SHOCK_LETTERS, col=1)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, path.pi[1], "", col=1)
    # panel (b): the path on to C
    add_event_path(fig, path, 2, SHOCK_LETTERS, col=2)
    # Step 4: the title reports where AS2 starts, and point C
    now = path.loc[2]
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"Period 2: AS₂ starts from π₁ = {path.pi[1]:.2f}%; "
        f"C: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {now.Y:.2f}%",
        panels=2,
    )
    return fig

                  description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
    nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25,

What to notice.

  • AS₂ lies between the original AS and AS₁: the shock is gone, but expected inflation is still 3 percent.
  • At \(C\) inflation is 2.5 percent and output is −0.5 percent: both gaps are half of what they were at \(B\).
  • The economy improves, but slowly. The same sticky expectations that keep inflation high keep the economy in a slump.

What to notice.

  • The steps get shorter: the economy moves fastest when it is furthest from the steady state, the same principle of transition dynamics as in the Solow model.
  • By period 6 or so the AS curve is hard to tell apart from the original one.

Fig. 9: The effects of an inflation shock: summary

Goal. See the whole event at once, in the AS/AD diagram and over time.

Panel (a) is the textbook’s summary: the jump from \(A\) to \(B\), then the slow return along the AD curve back to \(A\). Panel (b) adds the same path as two time series, so you can read how long the stagflation lasts. One function draws the summaries of all three events (Figs. 9, 11 and 15).

Two numbers sum up the event: the peak of inflation, and the sum of output over all periods, the total recession of equation (8). inflation_shock_episode simulates the event and computes both.

def inflation_shock_episode(o, m, nu):
    """The whole inflation-shock episode, and its two key numbers (Fig. 9).

    Equations (5) and (6) period by period (simulate); the sum of output is the
    total recession of equation (8), -o-bar / nu-bar

    Arguments
        o  : the inflation shock in period 1, o-bar
        m  : the policy response, m-bar
        nu : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        path  : the simulated event, one row per period
        peak  : the highest inflation rate, in percent
        total : the sum of output Y~ over all periods
    """
    # the shock o hits in period 1 only
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(o, 1), m=m, nu=nu)
    # the peak of inflation, and the total recession (equation 8)
    peak = path.pi.max()
    total = path.Y.sum()
    return path, peak, total
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Figs. 9, 11 and 15, inflation and output over time
def add_time_paths(fig, path, col=2):
    """Inflation and output over time, with the inflation target, in panel col.

    Panel (b) of Figs. 9, 11 and 15.

    Arguments
        fig  : the two-panel figure
        path : the simulated event, a table from simulate
        col  : the panel to draw in
    """
    # Step 1: inflation and output, one dot per period
    inflation = go.Scatter(
        x=path.period,
        y=path.pi,
        name="Inflation π",
        mode="lines+markers",
        line=dict(color=BLUE, width=3),
    )
    fig.add_trace(inflation, row=1, col=col)
    output = go.Scatter(
        x=path.period,
        y=path.Y,
        name="Output Ỹ",
        mode="lines+markers",
        line=dict(color=GREEN, width=3),
    )
    fig.add_trace(output, row=1, col=col)
    # Step 2: the target, a dotted gray line
    target = go.Scatter(
        x=[0, T_MAX],
        y=[path.target[1], path.target[1]],
        name="Target π̄",
        mode="lines",
        line=dict(color=GRAY, width=2, dash="dot"),
    )
    fig.add_trace(target, row=1, col=col)
    # Step 3: the axes; the vertical one wider than -3 to 7 only if a path leaves it
    fig.update_xaxes(
        title_text="Period",
        range=[-0.5, T_MAX + 0.5],
        tickvals=[0, 5, 10, 15, 20],
        row=1,
        col=col,
    )
    low = min(-3, path.Y.min() - 0.5, path.pi.min() - 0.5)
    high = max(7, path.pi.max() + 0.5)
    fig.update_yaxes(
        title_text="Percent",
        range=[low, high],
        tickvals=list(range(-12, 14, 2)),
        row=1,
        col=col,
    )
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 9, the summary of an event and of the inflation shock
def event_summary(path, letters, as_periods, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The whole path in the AS/AD diagram (a) and the same path over time (b).

    Draws Figs. 9, 11 and 15 (adapted from Figs. 13.9, 13.11 and 13.15 in Jones),
    without their titles.

    Arguments
        path       : the simulated event, a table from simulate
        letters    : {period: letter}, the textbook's letters
        as_periods : the periods whose AS curves are drawn
        m          : the policy response, m-bar
        nu         : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # panel (a): the AS/AD diagram with the whole path; panel (b): the time paths
    titles = ("(a) The AS/AD diagram", "(b) Inflation and output over time")
    fig = asad_figure(2, titles)
    add_event_curves(fig, path, T_MAX, as_periods, m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, T_MAX, letters)
    add_time_paths(fig, path)
    return fig


def inflation_shock_summary(o=2.0, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """A one-period inflation shock o, from the jump to B back to the steady state A.

    Draws Fig. 9 (adapted from Fig. 13.9 in Jones).

    Arguments
        o  : the inflation shock in period 1, o-bar
        m  : the policy response, m-bar
        nu : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the episode and its numbers (inflation_shock_episode)
    path, peak, total = inflation_shock_episode(o, m, nu)
    # Step 2: both panels, with the letter B and the AS curve of period 1
    fig = event_summary(path, {1: "B"}, [1], m, nu)
    # Step 3: the title reports the peak and the total recession
    total = round(total, 2) + 0.0                    # + 0.0 avoids "-0.00"
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"Shock ō = {o:.1f}: inflation peaks at {peak:.2f}%; sum of Ỹ = {total:.2f}",
    )
    return fig
# Fig. 9 with sliders for the shock and the two parameters
interact(
    inflation_shock_summary,
    o=FloatSlider(value=2.0, min=-2.0, max=4.0, step=0.5,
                  description="inflation shock ō", style=WIDE),
    m=FloatSlider(value=0.5, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25,
                  description="policy response m̄", style=WIDE),
    nu=FloatSlider(value=1.0, min=0.25, max=2.0, step=0.25,
                   description="AS slope ν̄", style=WIDE),
);
Show the code of the website version

slider_figure(

    "nu",
    [0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0],     # the values of nu-bar
    start=1.0,

Source. Adapted from Fig. 13.9 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed. Panel (b), the time paths of inflation and output, is our addition.

What to notice.

  • The shock lasts one period, but inflation stays above target for many periods, and output stays below potential all that time. Price shocks are insidious because they raise expected inflation.
  • The sum of output over all periods is −2.00: the total recession needed to undo the shock. A flatter AS curve (smaller \(\bar{\nu}\)) makes it longer and costlier, because prices then react less to a slump.
  • Change \(\bar{m}\): the recession becomes deeper but shorter, and the sum of output barely moves.

Key numbers: the inflation gap halves every period

With \(\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu} = 1\), the AS/AD solution makes the gap between inflation and the target shrink by the factor \(1/(1 + \bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu}) = 1/2\) each period (equation 7).

# The inflation shock, period by period, with the gap to the target
path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, shock_list(2.0, 1))
path["gap"] = path.pi - PI_BAR                   # inflation minus the target
# this period's gap divided by last period's: `path.gap.shift(1)` moves the
# column down by one row, so each row sees last period's gap
path["gap ratio"] = path.gap / path.gap.shift(1)
# `path.loc[0:6, [...]]` keeps rows 0 to 6 and the listed columns
path.loc[0:6, ["period", "Y", "pi", "gap", "gap ratio"]].round(3)
period Y pi gap gap ratio
0 0 0.000 2.000 0.000 NaN
1 1 -1.000 3.000 1.000 inf
2 2 -0.500 2.500 0.500 0.5
3 3 -0.250 2.250 0.250 0.5
4 4 -0.125 2.125 0.125 0.5
5 5 -0.062 2.062 0.062 0.5
6 6 -0.031 2.031 0.031 0.5

From period 2 on the ratio is exactly 0.5. (Period 0 has no gap, so the ratio of period 1 divides by zero and pandas shows inf.) Inflation is 3, 2.5, 2.25, … and output −1, −0.5, −0.25, …

Your turn. Over all periods, the total change in inflation is zero (it starts and ends at 2 percent). Use the AS curve to explain why the sum of output must then be \(-\bar{o}/\bar{\nu} = -2\) (equation 8). Check it with path.Y.sum().

Hint

Add up \(\pi_t - \pi_{t-1} = \bar{\nu}\tilde{Y}_t + \bar{o}_t\) over all periods. The left side adds up to zero, and the shock appears only once.

13.6 Event 2: disinflation

Now the central bank lowers its inflation target. Because expectations adjust slowly, getting inflation down costs a recession along the way.

Fig. 10: The initial response to disinflation

Goal. See Event #2: the central bank lowers its inflation target, as Paul Volcker’s Fed did in the 1980s.

The economy starts in a steady state with a target, and inflation, of 4 percent. The central bank now adopts a new rule with the target \(\bar{\pi}' = 2\) percent. The target appears only in the AD curve, so AD shifts down to AD₁: at any inflation rate the new rule wants lower output. Inflation of 4 percent is now “too high”, the real interest rate rises, and the economy moves from \(A\) to \(B\). The function reuses add_event_curves and add_event_path: only the event changes.

It simulates the event with simulate, so all of its code is drawing code.

Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 10, the economy t periods after the target is cut
def disinflation(pi_new=2.0, t=1, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS/AD diagram t periods after the target is cut from PI_OLD to pi_new.

    Draws Fig. 10 (adapted from Figs. 13.10 and 13.11 in Jones); from period 2 on,
    it also marks the new steady state C.

    Arguments
        pi_new : the new inflation target, pi-bar'
        t      : the period shown
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        nu     : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: simulate the event: inflation starts at PI_OLD, the target is pi_new
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, NO_SHOCK, PI_OLD, pi_new, m, nu)
    # Step 2: the curves of periods 1 to t, the path so far, and C after period 1
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_event_curves(fig, path, t, list(range(1, t + 1)), m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, t, {1: "B"})
    if t > 1:
        add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_new, "C")             # the new steady state
    # Step 3: the title reports period t (+ 0.0 avoids "-0.00")
    now = path.loc[t]
    Y_now = round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"Target {PI_OLD:.1f} → {pi_new:.1f}%.  "
        f"Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {Y_now:.2f}%",
    )
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 13.10 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Cutting the target by 2 points shifts AD down by exactly 2 points: AD₁ crosses \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) at the new target.
  • In period 1, inflation falls only to 3 percent, halfway between the old and the new target, and output falls 1 percent below potential.
  • The AS curve has not moved yet: firms still expect 4 percent inflation. Move the period slider to see it shift.

Fig. 11: The dynamics of disinflation

Goal. Follow the disinflation to the new steady state \(C\).

After period 1, firms expect lower inflation, so the AS curve shifts down period by period, just as after the inflation shock. The economy slides down AD₁ from \(B\) to the new steady state \(C\), where inflation equals the new target and output is back at potential. The summary function of Fig. 9 draws it; we add the point \(C\).

The key number is the output lost on the way, the cost of the disinflation (equation 8). disinflation_episode simulates the event and computes it.

def disinflation_episode(pi_new, m, nu):
    """The whole disinflation, and the output it costs (Fig. 11).

    Equations (5) and (6) period by period (simulate); by equation (8), the output
    lost is close to (pi-bar - pi-bar') / nu-bar

    Arguments
        pi_new : the new inflation target, pi-bar'
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        nu     : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        path : the simulated event, one row per period
        loss : the output lost over all periods, in percent of potential output
    """
    # inflation starts at the old target PI_OLD; the new target is pi_new
    path = simulate(NO_SHOCK, NO_SHOCK, PI_OLD, pi_new, m, nu)
    # the output lost: minus the sum of output over all periods
    loss = -path.Y.sum()
    return path, loss
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 11, the dynamics of disinflation
def disinflation_summary(pi_new=2.0, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """From A through B to the new steady state C, in the diagram and over time.

    Draws Fig. 11 (adapted from Fig. 13.11 in Jones).

    Arguments
        pi_new : the new inflation target, pi-bar'
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        nu     : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the episode and its cost (disinflation_episode)
    path, loss = disinflation_episode(pi_new, m, nu)
    # Step 2: both panels, with the letter B, the last AS curve and the point C
    fig = event_summary(path, {1: "B"}, [T_MAX], m, nu)
    add_point(fig, 0.0, pi_new, "C")
    # Step 3: the title reports the output lost
    loss = round(loss, 2) + 0.0                      # + 0.0 avoids "-0.00"
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"Target {PI_OLD:.1f} → {pi_new:.1f}%: "
        f"output lost over {T_MAX} periods = {loss:.2f}%",
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

  • Inflation falls for good, from 4 to 2 percent, and output returns to potential. The price is a recession: about 2 percent of a year’s output in total.
  • A more aggressive central bank (higher \(\bar{m}\)) makes the recession deeper and shorter, but the total loss stays near 2. Only the AS slope \(\bar{\nu}\) changes it: the total loss is \((\bar{\pi} - \bar{\pi}')/\bar{\nu}\) (equation 8).
  • Why must there be a recession at all? Because firms keep expecting the old inflation. If everyone believed the new target at once, the economy could jump straight from \(A\) to \(C\). Fig. 20 returns to this idea.

13.7 Event 3: a positive aggregate demand shock

A temporary spending boom raises output and inflation. When the boom ends, the higher inflation it left behind has to be squeezed out with a recession.

Fig. 12: A positive aggregate demand shock

Goal. See the first period of Event #3: a boom in demand, for example from a boom in Europe that raises the demand for U.S. exports.

A positive \(\bar{a}\) shifts the AD curve out to AD₁: at every inflation rate, output is higher. Firms see the extra demand and raise their prices, so the economy moves up the AS curve from \(A\) to \(B\). Part of the shock shows up as more output, part as more inflation. In our baseline the shock \(\bar{a} = 2\) lasts nine periods. One function draws Figs. 12 to 14, with the textbook’s letters \(B\), \(C\) and \(D\) at periods 1, 8 and 10.

The function below simulates the event with simulate and draws period \(t\), so all of its code is drawing code.

Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Figs. 12 to 14, the economy t periods after a demand shock
# the textbook's letters for periods 1, 8 and 10
DEMAND_LETTERS = {1: "B", 8: "C", 10: "D"}


def demand_shock(a=2.0, t=1, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """The AS/AD diagram t periods after a demand shock a that lasts to period A_LAST.

    Draws Figs. 12 to 14 (adapted from Figs. 13.12 to 13.14 in Jones).

    Arguments
        a  : the demand shock in periods 1 to A_LAST, a-bar
        t  : the period shown
        m  : the policy response, m-bar
        nu : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: simulate the event: the shock a lasts from period 1 to A_LAST
    path = simulate(shock_list(a, A_LAST), NO_SHOCK, m=m, nu=nu)
    # Step 2: the curves of periods 1 to t, and the path so far
    fig = asad_figure()
    add_event_curves(fig, path, t, list(range(1, t + 1)), m, nu)
    add_event_path(fig, path, t, DEMAND_LETTERS)
    # Step 3: the title reports period t (+ 0.0 avoids "-0.00")
    now = path.loc[t]
    Y_now = round(now.Y, 2) + 0.0
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"Period {t}: π = {now.pi:.2f}%, Ỹ = {Y_now:.2f}%   "
        f"(ā = {a:.1f} in periods 1–{A_LAST})",
    )
    return fig

What to notice.

  • A shock of 2 points raises output by 1 percent and inflation by 1 point, to 3 percent: again half and half.
  • A negative \(\bar{a}\) is a fall in demand: output and inflation both fall.
  • The economy cannot stay at \(B\). Inflation is above what firms expected, so the AS curve will shift. Which way? Fig. 13 answers.

Fig. 13: Dynamics as the AS curve shifts

Goal. See that while the demand shock lasts, the economy drifts to higher inflation, not back to \(A\).

Inflation at \(B\) is above the 2 percent firms expected, so next period they expect 3 percent, and the AS curve shifts up. Period by period, inflation rises and output falls back toward zero, along AD₁. At \(C\) (period 8 in the textbook) output is back at potential, but inflation is well above target. There \(\tilde{Y} = 0\) on AD₁, so (equation 9)

\[0 = \bar{a} - \bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi^c - \bar{\pi}) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \pi^c = \bar{\pi} + \frac{\bar{a}}{\bar{b}\bar{m}}.\]

It is the same demand_shock function, now at \(t = 8\).

Fig. 14: The unraveling after the aggregate demand shock ends

Goal. See what happens when the boom ends: a recession.

Demand shocks are temporary: in the long run \(\bar{a} = 0\), because the shares of output must add up to 1. Output was already at potential, so this works like a negative shock: the economy jumps from \(C\) to \(D\), below potential. The recession then pulls inflation down, the AS curve shifts down period by period, and the economy slides down the original AD curve back to \(A\). Again the same function, now at \(t = 10\).

Fig. 15: A positive aggregate demand shock: summary

Goal. See the whole boom-and-bust cycle, and what happens if the shock ends sooner.

The economy jumps from \(A\) to \(B\), drifts to \(C\), jumps to \(D\) when the shock ends, and returns to \(A\): a counterclockwise loop. The textbook lets the economy reach \(C\) before the boom ends, but the boom could end sooner. The slider sets the last period of the shock; the letters \(C\) and \(D\) mark that period and the next one.

Two numbers sum up the cycle: the peak of inflation, and the sum of output over all periods. demand_shock_episode simulates the event and computes both.

def demand_shock_episode(a, last, m, nu):
    """The boom-and-bust cycle of a demand shock, and its two key numbers (Fig. 15).

    Equations (5) and (6) period by period (simulate), with the shock a in periods 1
    to last

    Arguments
        a    : the demand shock, a-bar
        last : the last period of the shock
        m    : the policy response, m-bar
        nu   : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        path  : the simulated event, one row per period
        peak  : the highest inflation rate, in percent
        total : the sum of output Y~ over all periods (the boom minus the recession)
    """
    # the shock a lasts from period 1 to last
    path = simulate(shock_list(a, last), NO_SHOCK, m=m, nu=nu)
    # the peak of inflation, and the sum of output over the whole cycle
    peak = path.pi.max()
    total = path.Y.sum()
    return path, peak, total
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 15, the summary of a demand shock
def demand_shock_summary(a=2.0, last=A_LAST, m=M_BAR, nu=NU_BAR):
    """A demand shock a in periods 1 to last, in the AS/AD diagram and over time.

    Draws Fig. 15 (adapted from Fig. 13.15 in Jones).

    Arguments
        a    : the demand shock, a-bar
        last : the last period of the shock
        m    : the policy response, m-bar
        nu   : the slope of the AS curve, nu-bar
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the episode and its numbers (demand_shock_episode)
    path, peak, total = demand_shock_episode(a, last, m, nu)
    # Step 2: both panels; C and D mark the last period of the shock and the next
    letters = {1: "B", last: "C", last + 1: "D"}
    fig = event_summary(path, letters, [last], m, nu)
    # Step 3: the title reports the peak and the sum of output
    total = round(total, 2) + 0.0                    # + 0.0 avoids "-0.00"
    asad_axes(
        fig,
        f"ā = {a:.1f} in periods 1–{last}: π peaks at {peak:.2f}%; "
        f"sum of Ỹ = {total:.2f}",
    )
    return fig

Source. Adapted from Fig. 13.15 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • The path runs counterclockwise: up and to the right (boom, rising inflation), up and to the left, then down and to the left (recession, falling inflation), and back.
  • The sum of output over the whole cycle is about zero: the boom and the recession cancel out. What remains is a long period of high inflation, a net cost. That is why central banks try to stabilize output.
  • End the shock early (2 or 3 periods): the loop is smaller, and inflation peaks lower.

13.8 Empirical evidence

How well does the model describe real economies? We compare the fed funds rate with a simple policy rule, look for counterclockwise inflation-output loops, and see how forecasters missed the Great Recession.

Fig. 16: The fed funds rate, actual and predicted

Goal. Test the policy rule on U.S. data: does it predict the Federal Reserve’s interest rate?

The rule sets the real interest rate, but the Fed sets a nominal rate, the fed funds rate. The Fisher equation links the two, \(i_t = R_t + \pi_t\), so the rule implies (equation 10)

\[i_t = \bar{r} + \pi_t + \bar{m}\,(\pi_t - \bar{\pi}).\]

John Taylor picked numbers that are all built on the number 2: \(\bar{r} = 2\%\), \(\bar{m} = 1/2\) and \(\bar{\pi} = 2\%\). Then \(i_t = 1 + 1.5\,\pi_t\): when inflation rises by 1 point, the nominal rate rises by 1.5 points, so the real rate rises too. For inflation we use core PCE inflation (prices of consumer spending without food and energy), the measure that reproduces the textbook’s line.

# Load the data of Fig. 16. `pd.read_csv` reads a data file into a DataFrame, a
# table with named columns; `parse_dates=["date"]` turns text such as
# "1960-01-01" into real dates, and `.tail()` shows the last five rows
taylor = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "taylor_rule.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
taylor.tail()
date fed_funds core_inflation
262 2025-07-01 4.2933 2.8371
263 2025-10-01 3.8967 2.7661
264 2026-01-01 3.6400 3.0012
265 2026-04-01 3.6333 3.0956
266 2026-07-01 3.6700 NaN

Each row is a quarter. fed_funds is the average fed funds rate in the quarter, and core_inflation is the core PCE inflation rate over the last four quarters, both in percent. The last row has no inflation yet: the data for that quarter were not published when the file was made. The rule will simply stop one quarter earlier.

The same test works for other central banks. The file taylor_rule_countries.csv has, for 33 economies, the quarterly average of the central bank’s policy rate (from the Bank for International Settlements) and core inflation, the consumer price index without food and energy (from the OECD). For the United States it repeats the table above.

# Load the policy rates and core inflation of 33 economies
rules = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "taylor_rule_countries.csv", parse_dates=["date"])
# the first and the last quarter with both series, for the first eight economies:
# `.groupby("country")` splits the table by country, and `.agg(["min", "max"])`
# gives the earliest and the latest date of each
rules.dropna().groupby("country").date.agg(["min", "max"]).head(8)

Look at your data. The coverage differs a lot. Germany, France, Italy and the other early euro members have their own policy rate only until 1998, and the euro area from 1999; core inflation starts in the 1970s or 1990s in many countries, and for Japan it stops in mid-2021. Israel and Mexico in the 1980s and Türkiye in the 1990s and 2020s had very high inflation, so the rule asks for rates far off the chart.

The policy rule of equation (10) becomes a short function, policy_rule, that works on one inflation rate or on a whole column of them.

def policy_rule(pi, r_bar=2.0, m=M_BAR, pi_bar=PI_BAR):
    """The nominal interest rate that the policy rule sets.

    Equation (10):  i = r-bar + pi + m-bar (pi - pi-bar)

    Arguments
        pi     : inflation, in percent (one number or a whole column)
        r_bar  : the real interest rate in the long run, r-bar
        m      : the policy response, m-bar
        pi_bar : the inflation target, pi-bar
    Returns
        the nominal interest rate i, in percent
    """
    # the Fisher equation, i = R + pi, turns the rule for R into a rule for i
    return r_bar + pi + m * (pi - pi_bar)

fed_funds_data prepares the chart for one economy: its actual rate, the rate the rule predicts, and the average gap between the two since 2009.

def fed_funds_data(r_bar, m, country):
    """The actual policy rate of one economy, the rule's rate, and their gap (Fig. 16).

    Equation (10), computed by policy_rule, with the economy's core inflation

    Arguments
        r_bar   : r-bar in the rule
        m       : m-bar in the rule
        country : the economy, e.g. "United States"
    Returns
        chart  : a table with the date, the actual rate and the rule's rate
        actual : the name of the actual rate's column
        gap    : actual minus rule, average since 2009, in points (NaN: no data)
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the economy; for the U.S. the rate is the fed funds rate
    part = rules[rules.country == country]
    actual = "Actual policy rate"
    if country == "United States":
        actual = "Actual fed funds rate"
    # Step 2: one table with both rates
    chart = pd.DataFrame(
        {
            "date": part.date,
            actual: part.policy_rate,
            "Policy rule": policy_rule(part.core_inflation, r_bar, m),
        }
    )
    # Step 3: the average gap since 2009; + 0.0 turns a rounded -0.00 into 0.00
    since_2009 = (chart[actual] - chart["Policy rule"])[chart.date >= "2009-01-01"]
    gap = round(since_2009.mean(), 2) + 0.0
    return chart, actual, gap
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 16, the actual policy rate and the rule
def fed_funds_chart(r_bar=2.0, m=M_BAR, country="United States"):
    """The actual policy rate of one economy and the rate predicted by the policy rule.

    Draws Fig. 16 (inspired by Fig. 13.16 in Jones).

    Arguments
        r_bar   : r-bar in the rule
        m       : m-bar in the rule
        country : the economy, e.g. "United States"
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data of the chart (fed_funds_data)
    chart, actual, gap = fed_funds_data(r_bar, m, country)
    lines = chart[[actual, "Policy rule"]]
    # Step 2: the vertical axis: -1 to 22, wider only when an economy needs it
    low, high, ticks = -1, 22, [0, 4, 8, 12, 16, 20]
    for wider_low, wider_high, wider_ticks in [(-5, 45, None), (-10, 110, None)]:
        if lines.min().min() < low or lines.max().max() > high:
            low, high, ticks = wider_low, wider_high, wider_ticks
    # Step 3: the title reports the gap; `np.isnan(gap)` is true when there were
    # no quarters to average
    title = (
        f"Rule with r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}, m̄ = {m:.2f}: "
        f"actual minus rule since 2009 = {gap:.2f} points"
    )
    if np.isnan(gap):
        title = f"Rule with r̄ = {r_bar:.1f}, m̄ = {m:.2f} (no data since 2009)"
    # the legend's title: the economy, with a note when a line leaves the chart
    off = lines.min().min() < low or lines.max().max() > high
    legend = country + (" (off the chart)" if off else "")
    # Step 4: `px.line` with a list `y=[...]` draws one line per column
    fig = px.line(
        chart,
        x="date",
        y=[actual, "Policy rule"],
        color_discrete_sequence=[BLUE, GREEN],
        title=title,
        labels={"date": "Year", "value": "Percent", "variable": "Series"},
    )
    fig.update_traces(line_width=2.5)
    # the rule dashed: `selector=dict(name=...)` changes only the trace of that name
    fig.update_traces(line_dash="dash", selector=dict(name="Policy rule"))
    # Step 5: the axes and the legend
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis_range=["1958-01-01", "2027-12-31"],
        yaxis=dict(range=[low, high], tickvals=ticks),
        legend=dict(x=0.99, y=0.99, xanchor="right", yanchor="top"),
        legend_title_text=legend,
    )
    return fig

Sources. Data: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Federal Funds Effective Rate (FEDFUNDS), via FRED; U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, PCE price index excluding food and energy (JCXFE), via FRED; for the other economies, Bank for International Settlements, central bank policy rates (WS_CBPOL) and OECD, Consumer price indices, CPI excluding food and energy (DSD_PRICES@DF_PRICES_ALL), via the OECD Data Explorer. Prepared files: data/ch13/taylor_rule.csv and data/ch13/taylor_rule_countries.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 13.16 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

On the website, the second chart offers the 33 economies, with Taylor’s numbers r̄ = 2 and m̄ = 1/2.

What to notice.

  • The simple rule follows the big swings of the actual rate surprisingly well: the rise in the 1970s, the peak around 1980, and the long decline afterward.
  • From the late 1960s to 1980 the actual rate was well below the rule: monetary policy was too loose, and inflation rose through the 1970s.
  • In recessions (early 1990s, early 2000s and above all after 2008) the Fed set rates far below the rule. The full Taylor rule also responds to output, which explains part of this.
  • Lower \(\bar{r}\) to 1 or 0.5 percent, as many economists now do: the rule comes closer after 2008, but in 2021–2022 it still calls for rates far above the actual ones. The Fed raised rates late after the Covid-19 pandemic.
  • Choose the euro area, the United Kingdom or Canada: the same pattern. Their central banks also kept rates below the rule after 2009 (by 2.2, 3.3 and 2.6 points on average from 2009 to 2020) and even more in 2021–2022 (by 4.7, 5.9 and 5.5 points). The rule uses core consumer prices for them, not the core PCE index of the U.S. line.

Key numbers: how closely does the Fed follow the rule?

We average the gap between the actual rate and the rule over five episodes, and measure how closely the two rates move together.

# Step 1: the rule's rate in every quarter, and the actual rate minus the rule
taylor["rule"] = policy_rule(taylor.core_inflation)
taylor["gap"] = taylor.fed_funds - taylor.rule
# Step 2: the average gap in five episodes;
# `taylor[(taylor.date >= start) & (taylor.date <= end)]` keeps the quarters
# between two dates
for start, end in [
    ("1967", "1980-12-31"),
    ("1990", "1993-12-31"),
    ("2001", "2004-12-31"),
    ("2009", "2020-12-31"),
    ("2021", "2022-12-31"),
]:
    part = taylor[(taylor.date >= start) & (taylor.date <= end)]
    print(
        f"{start}-{end[:4]}: actual minus rule = "
        f"{part.gap.mean():+.2f} points on average"
    )
# Step 3: the correlation over the textbook's years. `.corr()` gives the
# correlation between two columns: 1 means they move perfectly together
book_span = taylor[taylor.date <= "2023-01-01"]
print(
    "Correlation of the actual rate with the rule, 1960Q1-2023Q1: "
    f"{book_span.fed_funds.corr(book_span.rule):.2f}"
)
# Step 4: the highest rate the rule asked for. `idxmax()` gives the row number of
# the largest value, and `:%Y-%m` in an f-string writes a date as year-month
print(
    f"Highest rule rate: {taylor.rule.max():.2f}% "
    f"in {taylor.date[taylor.rule.idxmax()]:%Y-%m}"
)
1967-1980: actual minus rule = -2.29 points on average
1990-1993: actual minus rule = -0.94 points on average
2001-2004: actual minus rule = -1.67 points on average
2009-2020: actual minus rule = -2.71 points on average
2021-2022: actual minus rule = -6.74 points on average
Correlation of the actual rate with the rule, 1960Q1-2023Q1: 0.75
Highest rule rate: 16.15% in 1975-01

The actual rate was below the rule by 2.3 points on average from 1967 to 1980, by 2.7 points from 2009 to 2020, and by 6.7 points in 2021–2022. The correlation of 0.75 says the two lines move together most of the time.

Fig. 17: Inflation-output loops in the U.S. economy

Goal. Look for the model’s counterclockwise loops in U.S. data.

The model predicts that the economy moves in counterclockwise loops in a diagram with output on the horizontal axis and inflation on the vertical axis (Fig. 15): a boom raises inflation, high inflation leads the central bank to cause a recession, and the recession brings inflation down. Each point below is one year: the output gap \(\tilde{Y}\) (actual GDP relative to the Congressional Budget Office’s estimate of potential GDP) and CPI inflation.

# Load the data of Fig. 17, and show four years: `.isin([...])` is true for the
# rows whose value is in the list
loops = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "loops_vintages.csv")
loops[loops.year.isin([2009, 2021, 2022, 2025])]
year inflation output_gap output_gap_2023
49 2009 -0.3204 -4.6619 -5.2000
61 2021 4.6812 0.8132 -1.2862
62 2022 7.9908 0.9160 -1.0390
65 2025 2.7058 1.3961 NaN

There are two output-gap columns. output_gap uses today’s data; output_gap_2023 uses the data as they were published in March 2023, when the textbook was written. GDP and, above all, the CBO’s potential GDP get revised: today’s estimate of potential output for 2021 is lower, so the same year now looks like a small boom (+0.8 percent) instead of a slump (−1.3 percent). The textbook’s data stop in 2022, so output_gap_2023 is empty (NaN) after that. Always check which vintage of the data a claim is based on.

# Step 1: the settings of the two periods: the first and the last year, the
# ranges of the two axes, and the ticks of the vertical axis. A dictionary such
# as WINDOWS maps a name to its settings, and `WINDOWS[years]` looks them up
WINDOWS = {
    "1960–1985": (1960, 1985, [-8, 7], [0, 15], [2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 14]),
    "1985–2025": (1985, 2025, [-6, 3], [-1.5, 9], [0, 2, 4, 6, 8]),
}
# Step 2: the two vintages; the textbook used the March 2023 vintage
VINTAGES = {"Current data": "output_gap", "Textbook data": "output_gap_2023"}


def loops_data(years, vintage):
    """The years of one period that have an output gap in the chosen vintage (Fig. 17).

    Arguments
        years   : the period, a key of WINDOWS, e.g. "1960–1985"
        vintage : the data vintage, a key of VINTAGES
    Returns
        part   : the rows of those years, without missing output gaps
        column : the name of the output-gap column of that vintage
    """
    # Step 3: the first and the last year, and the column of the vintage
    first, last = WINDOWS[years][0], WINDOWS[years][1]
    column = VINTAGES[vintage]
    # Step 4: the rows of those years; `dropna` drops the years without a gap
    part = loops[(loops.year >= first) & (loops.year <= last)].dropna(subset=[column])
    return part, column
Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 17, inflation-output loops in the U.S.
# the years with a label (hover shows the others)
KEY_YEARS = [
    1960, 1966, 1969, 1974, 1975, 1979, 1980, 1982, 1985, 1989,
    1991, 2000, 2009, 2011, 2015, 2019, 2020, 2021, 2022, 2025,
]
# labels moved off nearby points
MOVED = {2020: "bottom center", 2021: "middle right", 2025: "bottom center"}


def loops_chart(years="1960–1985", vintage="Current data"):
    """Annual (output gap, inflation) points connected in time order.

    Draws Fig. 17 (inspired by Fig. 13.17 in Jones).

    Arguments
        years   : the period, a key of WINDOWS
        vintage : the data vintage, a key of VINTAGES
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the data (loops_data), and the axes of the period
    part, column = loops_data(years, vintage)
    first, last, x_range, y_range, y_ticks = WINDOWS[years]
    # Step 2: a label for the key years only. `.where(key, "")` keeps a value where
    # key is true and puts an empty text elsewhere; `.astype(str)` turns the years
    # into text, and `part.assign(label=...)` returns a copy with the new column
    key = part.year.isin(KEY_YEARS)
    part = part.assign(label=part.year.astype(str).where(key, ""))
    # Step 3: the points, connected in time order
    fig = px.line(
        part,
        x=column,
        y="inflation",
        text="label",
        markers=True,
        hover_name="year",
        labels={
            column: "Output gap, Ỹ (percent)",
            "inflation": "CPI inflation (percent)",
        },
        title=f"Counterclockwise loops, {first}–{part.year.max()} ({vintage.lower()})",
    )
    # Step 4: a label position for every year: `MOVED.get(year, "top center")`
    # looks up year in MOVED and gives "top center" when it is not there
    positions = []
    for year in part.year:
        positions.append(MOVED.get(year, "top center"))
    fig.update_traces(
        line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2),
        marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=7),
        textposition=positions,
    )
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis=dict(range=x_range, zeroline=True),
        yaxis=dict(range=y_range, tickvals=y_ticks),
    )
    return fig

Sources. Data: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, Real Gross Domestic Product (GDPC1), via FRED; Congressional Budget Office, Real Potential Gross Domestic Product (GDPPOT), via FRED; U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPIAUCSL), via FRED; the textbook vintage of GDP and potential GDP (30 March 2023) from ALFRED, the St. Louis Fed’s archive of past data vintages. Prepared file: data/ch13/loops_vintages.csv (see the data notes). Chart: inspired by Fig. 13.17 in Jones (2024), Macroeconomics, 6th ed.

What to notice.

  • Follow the years in 1960–1985: the boom of the late 1960s raises inflation, the high inflation of 1974–75 and 1979–80 is followed by deep recessions (1975, 1982), and inflation falls. The loops run counterclockwise, as the model predicts.
  • After 1985 the loops are smaller: the Great Moderation. The big exceptions are the deep slump of 2009–2011, during which inflation rose instead of falling, and the jump to 8 percent inflation in 2022.
  • Switch to the textbook data: the whole 1985–2022 cloud moves left by about 1 point. The shape of the loops is the same, but statements about the level of the gap depend on the vintage.

Key numbers: two vintages of the same year

The textbook says that in 2009 “output was more than 5 percent below potential”, and that inflation rose from 2009 to 2011 despite the slump.

# The 2009 output gap in the two vintages, and inflation from 2009 to 2011.
# `.set_index("year")` labels the rows by year, so `by_year.loc[2009, "inflation"]`
# picks one value
by_year = loops.set_index("year")
print(
    f"2009 output gap: {by_year.loc[2009, 'output_gap_2023']:.2f}% (textbook data), "
    f"{by_year.loc[2009, 'output_gap']:.2f}% (current data)"
)
print(
    f"Inflation 2009 -> 2011: {by_year.loc[2009, 'inflation']:.2f}% -> "
    f"{by_year.loc[2011, 'inflation']:.2f}%"
)
# the revision since 1985: the current gap minus the textbook's
revision = (loops.output_gap - loops.output_gap_2023)[loops.year >= 1985]
print(
    f"Current minus textbook output gap, 1985-2022: {revision.mean():.2f} points "
    f"on average, {revision.max():.2f} at most"
)
2009 output gap: -5.20% (textbook data), -4.66% (current data)
Inflation 2009 -> 2011: -0.32% -> 3.14%
Current minus textbook output gap, 1985-2022: 1.03 points on average, 2.10 at most

With the textbook’s data the 2009 gap is −5.20 percent; with today’s data it is −4.66 percent, so “more than 5 percent” is no longer true. Inflation did rise, from −0.32 to 3.14 percent, partly because of energy and commodity prices.

Loops in other countries

The OECD estimates the output gap of 40 economies, most of them since 1985, with one method for all. The file output_gaps_oecd.csv has these estimates, and inflation_annual.csv has CPI inflation for 194 economies (the World Bank’s numbers, and for the four economies of Fig. 19 the numbers of that figure). We join them by country and year. For the United States the OECD’s gap differs from the CBO’s: it is 0.2 points higher on average since 1985, and −3.98 percent in 2009 instead of −4.66. Potential output cannot be observed, so every estimate of the gap is a model.

# Load the OECD output gaps and the inflation rates, and join them. `merge` joins
# two tables on the columns they share, here `iso3` (a three-letter country
# code), `country` and `year`, and keeps the rows found in both
gaps = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "output_gaps_oecd.csv")
prices = pd.read_csv(DATA_URL + "inflation_annual.csv")

The function below draws the loops of one economy, as in Fig. 17, with axes that fit its data. It only picks the economy’s rows, so all of its code is drawing code.

Show the drawing code 
# @title Drawing code: Fig. 17, the loops of one economy, with OECD output gaps
def oecd_loops_chart(country="United States"):
    """Annual (output gap, inflation) points of one economy, with OECD output gaps.

    Draws Fig. 17, extended to other economies (inspired by Fig. 13.17 in Jones).

    Arguments
        country : the economy, e.g. "United States"
    Returns
        a Plotly figure
    """
    # Step 1: the rows of the economy, with a label every five years and in the last
    # year: `part.year % 5 == 0` is true for years that end in 0 or 5
    part = eo_loops[eo_loops.country == country]
    labeled = (part.year % 5 == 0) | (part.year == part.year.max())
    label = part.year.astype(str).where(labeled, "")
    # Step 2: axes that fit the data, with one point to spare on each side;
    # `np.floor` rounds down and `np.ceil` rounds up
    x_range = [np.floor(part.output_gap.min()) - 1, np.ceil(part.output_gap.max()) + 1]
    y_low = np.floor(min(part.inflation.min(), 0)) - 1
    y_range = [y_low, np.ceil(part.inflation.max()) + 1]
    # Step 3: the points, connected in time order
    fig = px.line(
        part.assign(label=label),
        x="output_gap",
        y="inflation",
        text="label",
        markers=True,
        hover_name="year",
        title=(
            f"{country}: inflation and the output gap, "
            f"{part.year.min()}–{part.year.max()}"
        ),
        labels={
            "output_gap": "Output gap, Ỹ (percent, OECD)",
            "inflation": "CPI inflation (percent)",
        },
    )
    fig.update_traces(
        line=dict(color=BLUE, width=2),
        marker=dict(color=TEAL, size=7),
        textposition="top center",
    )
    fig.update_layout(
        xaxis=dict(range=x_range, zeroline=True),
        yaxis=dict(range=y_range),
    )
    return fig
# The loops of one economy, with a menu for the country
interact(
    oecd_loops_chart,
    country=Dropdown(options=sorted(eo_loops.country.unique()), value="United States",
                     description="country", style=WIDE),
);
Show the code of the website version

menu_figure(

Fig. 18: Forecasting and the Great Recession

Goal. See how professional forecasters missed the Great Recession, quarter after quarter.

If economists understand fluctuations so well, can they forecast them? The Survey of Professional Forecasters, run by the Federal Reserve Bank of Philadelphia, asks experts every quarter for their forecast of U.S. employment. This figure stays U.S.-only: the survey covers only the U.S. economy, and the similar survey of the European Central Bank asks about growth, inflation and unemployment rates, not about the number of jobs. The economists James Stock and Mark Watson called this figure “the mother of all forecast errors”.

Each spf_... column is the median forecast made in one quarter (from 2007Q4 to 2009Q4) for that quarter and the next four; it is empty (NaN) elsewhere. For a chart with one line per series, we first reshape the table to long form: one row per date and series.

# Step 1: a readable name for every column. `spf.columns[2:]` is the list of
# column names from the third one on (the forecasts); `column[4:8]` takes the
# characters 4 to 7 of a text, here the year, and `column[-1]` its last
# character, here the quarter
NAMES = {"employment_actual": "Actual employment"}
for column in spf.columns[2:]:
    NAMES[column] = "Forecast made in " + column[4:8] + "Q" + column[-1]
# Step 2: the long form. `melt` stacks columns into rows: `id_vars="date"` stays
# a column, and the names of the other columns go into a new column `series`;
# `.dropna()` drops the quarters without a value
long = spf.melt(id_vars="date", var_name="series", value_name="employment").dropna()
# `.map(NAMES)` replaces each column name by its readable name from the dictionary
long["series"] = long.series.map(NAMES)

What to notice.

13.9 Modern monetary policy and inflation targeting

Inflation fell around the world after the 1980s. These figures show why expectations and credible targets matter so much, and how inflation in the United Kingdom has behaved over three centuries.

Fig. 19: Inflation in the OECD

Goal. Compare inflation in the U.S., the U.K., the euro area and Japan since 1960.

The U.S. Fed under Volcker, Greenspan, Bernanke and Yellen gets much credit for low inflation. But inflation fell just as much in other rich countries. Was it better policy, or good luck, such as no repeat of the 1970s oil shocks?
